NEW YEAR'S READING. WITH THE COMPLIMENTS OF THE

SEASON." - "You wish me 'A Happy New Year' as a toast, And a very kind act it appears; But-when you perceive rm as deaf as a post, You would wish me two happy new ears." WINTER EVENING. To-night the very horses springing by To gold from whitened nostrils. In a dream : The streets that narrow to the westward gleam Like rows of golden palaces; and high From all the crowded chimneys tower and die A thousand aureoles. Down in the west The brimming plains beneath the sunset rest, One burning sea of gold. Soon, soon shall fly The glorious vision, and the hours shall feel A mightier master; soon from height to height, With silence and the sharp unpitying stars, Stern creeping frosts and winds that touch like teel, Out of the depth beyond the eastern bars, Glittering and still, shall come the awful night. Scribner's Magazine. A. LAMPMAN'.

CHILDREN AND JESTS. Children hear the Gospels say What was Jesus' earthly way: Always loyal, always mild, With the little Hebrew child. Babies' love and children's song Follow Him His whole life long Boy and maid in glad surprise Fix on Him wide, wondering eyes. When they come one busy day, Men by whom they're sent away He rebukes in tender pain, Bids them call them back again. When His hand is on its prow, Baby says," I'm better now." When He touches blind boys' eyes, "Lo!" they say, "I see the skies!" Little faces, pinched with pain, Jesus makes so nice again. Homeless children, poor and sad, Be befriends, and they are glad. Sick, or well and out at play, Jesus loves them, every way, Never needing prophet's word To become the children's Lord. , Then the gentle Jesus dies, And is lost within the skies: He who was the children's friond, Who had loved them to the end. But, as stars we see at night Are the same when out of sight, So this Jesus is the same: Child is still His dearest name. So, the Bing of worlds above! King of children! King of love! As of earth, so now His prize, Children are of Paradise. —Little Snow-fakes.
SEASONABLE VARIETIES.

--- What instrnment is like a cutting reply ?—Ths retort. When is a window like a star P—When it's a skylight. What animal would you like to be on a cold day ? A little otter. Why is a person bathing in the river at Paris like a madman?—Because he's in Seine (insane). What pupil is the most to be pitied 7—The pupil of the eye, because it is always under the lash. Why should Africa rightly be considered to rank first of the continents P—Because it bears the palm. What is the difference between a brewer anal), flea?— The one buys hems and the other takes them. What is the queen of roses in the gardens 7—The rose of the watering-pot, for it rains over all otheris:r How can it be proved that a horse has stie legs ? Because he has fore legs in front and tyre behind. • What is that which Adam never saw, never possessed,' and yet he gave two to each of his childrerV—Parents. Why are crockeryware dealers unlike alreother shop- keepers P—Because it won't do for them to crack up their goods. Is there an English word that contains all the vowels? ----Unquestieuably. A teetotaller thinks that all "sensible people" would prefer them in their regular order— Abstemiously. A CCOSPROTHISE.—O'Roonev (entering hardware store) : "The boas sint me down afther a pane as' glass, tin be fourteen." Waggish Clerk : "Well, Pat, I don't think I can give you a ten-by-fourteen, but I can let you have a fourteen-by-ten, if you think you can make that do." Pat (struck with a bright idea) : "Be hivven ! jist gim- me wan av thim, and Oi'll jist turn th' sideways as' it upside down, an' Oi don't belave the boss himself ud ever know tie difference." "AT CHRTSTESIESSE-TTOF.." Two oorrie Thynges there be— . Ay, three:— A Neste from which ye Fledglings have been taken, A Lambe forsaken, rA redde leaf from ye Wilde Rose rudely shaken. Of gladde Thvnges there be more— Ay, four:— A Larke above ye olde Neste blithely singing, A wilde Rose clinging • In safety to a Rock. a Shepherds bringing A Lambe, found, iq his armes, and Chrystemesse Bells a-ringing, WARNING 'to WIDOWERS.—Another ghost story is much more fearful, and it is a warning to widowers not to forget their dead wives; at least, too BOOR after their departure. A man, who had just attended the funeral of his wife, went that same evening to court a young woman who lived in a cottage near the churchyard. The courtship proceeded with disgusting rapidity on both sides, and as they were laughing together, the girl's mother entered the room and rebuked the.pair for their heartless conduct. The widower turned the reproach aside with a flippant jest, when, chancing the next moment to look out of the window, he saw to his horror and amazement the face of his dead wife peering steadfastly at him. He immediately returned home, and in a fort- night was dead. The fearful apparition brought on an attack of brain fever, from whish he never recOvered.— Chatterbox Christmas Number. ASOAEDSREIDEN.—Another sort of legends that cluster round Christmas in Norway are those 'of " Asgards- reiden." When Christmas parties have become wild and noisy, quarrels and fights have arisen, and knives been drawn, then there suddenly is heard a rustle in the air, as of a coming storm, horse-hoofs trample on the roof of the house, tinkling of bells and bridles are heard above the clamour of the furious Christmas guests; and taken by invisible hands, the offenders are dragged out of the house, and hurled by the hair through the air, where they often vanish without any trace left. They are . taken by " AsgarJsreiden ;" and " Asgardsreiden " con- sists of all evil ghosts. which 'are doomed to this nightly ride without rest. These legends are relics of the. time when the old heathen gods were turned ovor to become evil spirits by the intruding Christianity. Therefore 'the name of this wild riding procession up in the • Clouds is called "Asgardsreiden;" for " Asgard " was the name of the abodes of the heathen gods. Many Nor- wegian peasants believe in and are afraid of " Asgards- reiden," especially when they have bad consciences; and _many have seen the horrid procession run with a fearful speed and deafening noise over the roofs of the houses • and tops of the trees, in a cloudy, stormy night. In acme places they still have preventive against "Asgards- feiden." Air FIONEST LITTLE MAN.—"It was the other - day," she said, "I was walking along one of the principal streets of Edinburgh, thinking to myself how bitterly cold it was for May. Spring has been late everywhere this year, but down here in the south, tholgh you may think you have had something be complain of, you can have no idea how Cold WO have had it; and the long light days seem to make it worse somehow Well, I was walking along quietly, when I • caught sight of a poor little boy hopping across the road. I say 'hopping,' because it ' gives you the best idea of the queer way he . got along, for he was terribly crippled, and his only way of moving was by something between a jerk and a hop on his crutches. And yet he managed to come to quickly. You would really have been amused to see the ' kind of fly he came with, and how cleverly he dodged and darted in and out' of the cabs and carriages, for it was the busiest time of the day. And fancy, children, his poor little legs and feet from his knees were quite bare. That is not a very unusual sight in Edinburgh, and not by any means at all times • rine to call forth pity. But in the case of my poor little cripple it was pitiful; for the weather was 30 cold, and the thin legs and feet so red, and the poor twisted-up one looked so specially unhappy. *Poor little boy,' .I exclaimed to the lady I was with; 'just look at ,him. Why, he has hopped all across the street merely for the pleasure of looking at the nice things in that window!' For by this time the boy was staring in 'with all his eyes at a confectioner's close to where we ' were passing. Give him a nenny, do,' said my friend, 'or go into the shop and buy him something.' We went close up to the boy, ' and I touched him on the shoulder. He looked up— such a pretty, happy face he had—and I said to him, Well, my man, which shall I give you, a penny or a cookie?' He smiled brightly, but you would never guess what he answered. Lice our' honest little man'

-Tie-";et," and Auntie patted Baby's head as she SP-Oie7tt-he held out his hand—not a dirty hand 'considering '—and -aaid cheerfully, 'Plenty to buy some wi', thank ye, •naem ; ' and spying into his hand I saw, children, ens halfpenny. 7 Auntie stopped. I think there •were tears in her eyes. "And what did you do, Auntie ?" we all cried. " ' What could I have done but • what I did ?' " she said. "I don't know if it would have

- • been better not—better to let his simple honesty be its own reward. I could not resist It; of course I gave him .another penny! He thanked me again quite simply: I .atn sure it never struck him that he had done anything to be praised for, and I didn't praise him—l just gave him a penny. And oh, how his bright eyes gleamed! fie looked now as if he thought he had wealth enough at his command to buy all the cookies in the shop."-4 ,ehristanas Poswity Mrs. Molestoorth. ,

THE STORY OF A LOVE LETTER; OR, THE "HAPPY OCCASION.' •It is New Year's Day. lamto be married this morning at 10.30. In fact, in exactly two hours and forty-five minutes the knot will be tied, and I—that is, She and Me—will be a "happy couple.." „. . .

. See, here are. all my wedding togs; what a swell I, shall look in 'em! If that coat, dove-coloured inexpres- sibles, and that remarkably sweet thing in neckties, don't make me gay, what will, I should like to know? Of course, I'm brimful of delight'; of course, I'm humming merry tunes; my heart is swelling proudly; my eyes are bright with anticipation! Why, what's this? Who is !hat woe-begone, wretched- looking individual staring out at me from the glass, with blood-shot eyes? Who is it? Why, its the happy bridegroom in ems— it's ME. "Confound it! There's the button off my shirt collar! How tight these new boots are! I couldn't sleep a wink last night ; tny.hand trembles so I can't shave—there, cut myself agam ! Da.sh it all ! " Why am n I going to wed this woman at 10-30; Is she pretty? Well, pretty well far that ...Am I fond of her? (love 2—pshaw : that's a word quite .of fashion nowadays.) I like her, and that'll serve,. won't it? Pm sure it does duty for the other thing pretty Often There, I'm dressed now. Mr. Poole's coat, dove- coloured inexpressibles—everything correct. I'm quite ready for the " happy occasion." But why am I going to be married? Well, I'll tell you. 1. I'm forty-eight years old. 2. I'm sick of furnished lodgings and tavern dinners. 3. My friends tell me I should settle down and "become respectable." But why don't I marry someone I could love I'll tell you about that also. 1. Because just about twenty-two years ago (on this very day) I was cruelly jilted by the only woman I ever loved. 2. I have never been able to go in for "that sort of thing" again. Ay, on this very day (what a bright, smiling morning it was! it's raining cats and dogs now) I wrote a letter, ' into which I put my whole heart and soul—a passionate, foolish, crude letter, doubtless, but the fervid words came straight from my heart, and should have met with, , at least, courtesy, ` She never took tfe sliglttest atice of it. Yet she let me understand that she loved me—very much. Ha, ha! She married my old schoolfellow, whom I recollect as Tones minor, the dullest, the greediest, and the ugliest boy in the Lower Fourth, just three months after I wrote that eventful letter Yes, it was rather eventful ; it only destroyed my life; but, bah! ain't I going to be married this morning, and ain't las jolly as possible at the prospect, though it does rain as if it would never leave off? * Fond! Ah, how fond I was of her! Sometimes, even now—well, not very long ago; in fact, only last night— the haunting deep blue eyes were looking at me, and their expression puzzled me, for it was reproachful. Ha, ha! Reproachful! And she jilted me in that shameful way. She hadn't even the politeness to break it to me kindly. She utterly ignored me—she didn't even answer my letter, by so much as one word! If she had only written a big No on a scrap of paper, and put it in the penny post—but she didn't think it worth even a Queen's head! And yet those deep blue eyes I would have done any- thing for—yes, I would, in those days—looked at me reproachfully from, I should say, about 3 a.m. to 8 ditto. "Come in!" Someone knocking at the door. It's my man, West, with an old, shabby-looking sort of writing-case in his hand, and he wants to know if it's to go with my other traps he is packing—for the honey- moon trip! gni I tell him, carelessly, " No, it's no use to me—he can have it, if he likes; but I'll just look at it first, and destroy the contents." He thanks me and goes. It isn't even locked; I don't suppose I've used it for years. Nothing here of any value. A quantity of old business letters, paid bills and memoranda of differ- ent sorts—all food for the lira. There, now West can have it— Stay, what's this? A bulky envelope, stamped and directed—ready, in fact, for the post.-...1t is lying upside down, but something—besides this faint, deadly sickness with the hard lump rising in my throat—tells me the Alfdress. Something—that has had life in my life for two-and-twenty years, and that is burning with as fierce a flame now as then—tells me what it is. ~. It is THE Lrrrzn, never posted—never sent to her! "If you please, sir, missis have sent to know if yort wasn't well, as the clergyman have gene on to the church some time, and they're all ready, waiting foryou !"

Lib o' owd Stuttin' Ailse's wur th' lass As owned a gret lump ov his heart; An' th' way as he'd glint when hoo'd pass, Showed he thowt her sweeter than tart. Sometimes he'd show t' whites ov his een, An' heyve a gret sigh, long an' deep.. At cooartin', hey! Noddy wur green,. An' seemed to be welly asleep! An' eyed her so lovin' an' fond. As simple an' quate as a child, When for a wawk-heawt hoo wur donn'd. Neaw, Lib, tho' hoo liked Neddv wee!, An' keered nowt for glitterin' "pell," Wur anxious to hear th' weddin' peal, An' ducirt'd want leovin' on t' shelf. 800 waited—an' waited i' vain— His offer e' GO Bear ; But they cooarted t' sunshine an' rain, Till Time rolled on into Loop Year! An' Leap Year wur gooin' on fast, Wod quare thowta hoo hed aw kornd tell, But iv Neddy sed nowt, at last Ho vowed as hoo'd ax him hersel. Well, th' neet after, Ned wawked th' heawse Au' seat kissel dea.wn th' arm:chear As staidly an' quate as a meawse, Fair lost, bekose Libby wornd thee?, Be waited awhile, Watchin' t' clock, • An' hearken'd fooak pasein' i th' street Then see his fair lass's owd frock th' corner, o drippin' wi' weet. " Wheer is hoo ?" he drawled, calm an' slaw, An' started to fidget a bit; " Goran eawt!" Ned just murmured gnat. "Oh An' then he'd another long sit. Then Lib coom in, mekkin a fuss, An' towd o'er two beawn to be wed; " Hey mam, they've nooan cooarted like us "Nome, nowe ! they'n mooar sense," owd Ailsesed. Lib tOed to draw Neddy to t' point, But th' chap wur too bothurd to see 't; 800 hinted as weddin' wur th' joint As med two lives happy an' breet. Owd Ailse pike?. off quately upstairs, An' sed hoo wur gain' to bed, When Lib shea.wted eawt, "0, ml cares May thicken, but, mam, aw'll be wed !" Ned seet still th' chear, like a fee, An' stared, wi' his rneawth wide agape, When Owd AiLse co'd back, "Ay! whoa to?" " Wey, to Ned here!" Lib ans'ered. " Come,shape,' Hoo sed to her chap; "tell her streyt, 800 thinks aw'm nod tellin' her true!" Ned simpered, as white as a sheet, • "lell happen be t' best iv we do !" Two months after thad th' job wur done, An' they rnek a weel-mated pair; They clung tooan to t' other, an' fun 0' th' joys o' this life a good share. An' Lib, when hoo's on for some chaff, Oft see, wi' a bit ov a leer, "Them lasses wi' chaps—neaw, dorn'd laff! Mun do t' same as me—it's beep Year JACK 0' ANN's.

IMPENDING STRIKE IN THE Ccrrrom Tuins.—The Bolton Operative Cotton Spinners' Association having refused to settle the dispute in the trade :on the employers' terms, the resolution to run short time three days a week came into force on Wednesday. Over thirty thousand opera- tives are affected. The employers threaten also that if the dispute remains unsettled a month hence a general lockout will be adopted. The operatives declare that the association has funds which would enable them to remain out twelve months without making a special levy,

mid she bad burst into a cyniclai laugh which 11 1 became her, when he tried to indulge in sentimental rubbish—and she assured him "it was no good losing his temper" when he made wild appeals to her for some pity. It was so much easier for her to keep command over her own emotion. There was something so large and moderate, so quiet and superior in her new way of looking at things that it effectually cooled his ardour, and much as he loved her he chafed at this manner,which was not natural t• her at other times, and which contrasted so oddly with the free and easy Ursula of the past. "Well," he said, a little sulkily, when he came to see her, soon after her last conversation with Field- ing, "so you can find something to say to me at last?" . . .

, She was very pale—and an alacrity which was evidently forced struck him in her manner. , "Ursula—you are suffering! You are keeping something back from me! " he said, trying feebly to utter something he had long been intending to say to her. She gazed at him with large eyes of wonder. He cleared his throat and made another effort. It was agonising to prolong the suspense. "There is a mistake somewhere," said the man, suddenly straightening himself with an air of greater nobility than he had ever shewn before, in spite of his assumption of a high flown tragedy manner, 'you do not care for me—you Care for this other fellow. I—l restore to you—your liberty." She smothered a cry of pain. She would have given a negative to his idea that she was suflering if she could have done so truthfully. As it was she said, "There is no other man." How was it possible for her to tell him that he had set her free too late, that the kind and gene. 'roes spirit which dictated his offer 'could no longer be of any use. There was not, as he supposed, a choice between rival candidates but the feeling of chilvalrous courtesy which made him ready to do justice to such supposed 'pretensions was no lees to his credit. Yet it was not in her 0 prevent send- ing a pang to his heart as she tried to explain. Marriage is a vocation; it is not mine you see. Nature meant me for different things:" It was wrong all round. Grandet would have gene back to Paris happier if he had not been deprived of his 'romance. As he told her he could have wished her a husband absolutely perfect—ideal; but the truth had been breaking upon him by degrees that he was not such &man. She, of eoaro,saLl utlring to Fielding of ALM/14 .hapPebed, and he had to ii a effort on himself not to come near her even when it seemed good for the sake of his work to do so. He knew that London would soon be solitary for him, and that he would have to keep his sorrow at arm's length daring the work of the day, and to conquer it when he paced the lamplit streets. To be enfranchised from the thraldom which his passion had begun to ex- ercise • ()Ter him w.ould indeed be something. Mean- while he would have been more than human if he could have been quite fair to Ursula. He could not help thinking of her somewhat jealously, as of onein whom new hopes would be stirring and fresh aspira- tions rising to make her forgetful of tl.e unhappiness of others. Meeting her accidentally at the house of a mutual friend one evening, he saw something new in her face which he could not understand, arid was half inclined to accuse her of being triumphant and unable to conceal it. It was after Grandet's departure. She was look- ing better than usual, and Fielding, who was feeding ill himself with old wales which were sore, and old wounds unhealed, thought as he hastily took his leave how under other circumstances he might have been able to refreih his eyes with her healthful ap- pearance. Seldom before had he seen such signs in her of a superabundant vitality. A few days 'afterwards he forced himself to call upon her on a matter entirely connected with business—the ease of a poor woman in whom they took' a mutual interest, and which, if not person- ally discussed would necessitate the writing ot many letters—and was surprised to find her in terms. She was still young enough to have her face softened by these team but lie tried, as usual, to silence his heart instead of questioning it, as he hastily apologised for his intrusion and 'prepared to withdraw OA coldly as before. "It was the servant's fault for shewing me up. You should have said 'Not at home 'if you had not cared to see me on business." "Indeed 1" stretching out her hand with her old hospitable gesture. "You are the very Person I was wishing to see." . He appreciated the effort she made to control her emotion, but the memories which rankled in his mind, prevented hint from answering her. ,He would have liked to remind her that there were questions it was Uf+2leFlig theln tOtlif3M3 any farther, Lei slid f4eVl'ldzi tO Inch reaiotten tTie ektatailZ;e of any sitch questions. Instead, to his great astonishment, she began in her old strain— " You are so good in helping everyone who is in trouble, I feel sure you will help rae stili—it is about thy larother." Pray , don't talk like that. f ~thought you, had given it up," he responded, with a queer smile resem- bling a „orimace. He would ha ye liked to remind her with a little irony haw Luther used to say, " I dread my good works mere than my wickedness," whilst, in fact, what lie dreaded were the praises of a woman. What was the use of equivocating about the thing, even to himself? He hated the congratulations of most women, but he was fool enough to feel his heart give a sort of bound at the intoxicating praises of this one. A minute or two before he had determined not to listen to her, but the allusion to her brothar turned the already wavering scale of his hesitation. He, too, had neglected the duty of speaking to her 1 about R,s„yrnond. I He could not pretend to have any appreciation of Grandet, and if she had tried to talk to him about her-love affairs, he must have listened to her with a pity which bordered almost on scorn. But this apprehension for her 'future was turned into his former reverence for her when be found that she had, as usual, forgotten herself, and that her tears were entirely for her brother. He need now have no delicate aversion to forcing her confidence. "You have heard," he said, "that he has left the Salvation Artny ? " "Yes ; iyhydid you not tell me before? He has i been all alone n Paris—consorting with men who are not likely to do him any good." "He could not have done so had you not supplied him with money. I begged you not to do it— entreated you with an argency which bordered on the impolite." "And I wet So obstinate ! " Her heart already smote her for her mistake. "Oh ! it was ray.fatit—and it was you wl-4,0 were right —as you Are alwaya tr! ce., With tha want of refitraiet Which had always been indre or less relaxed between them, "If it were only Pierre Dubois and hid Pset—:-bat I hear that Raymond is so freqliently at—at the—." She did ' not finish the sentence, and Fielding did not finish it for her. He had known for some weeks 'that Raymond, who had broken with his late as- sociates,was constantlyat a certain theatre where the actresses did net bear a good repute, that he had also begun to frequent gambling- houses, and that the WO more than reason to dread that his old in- temperate halals were regaining their asconditneY• "Campion is of age, now," he began; apa then, "Why will you force me to explain ?" There was a strange, excitedlook in her face; "It is not only that-one of my'old friends in Paris has written to warn ine,and that the letter came this Riming," she said, '" but that I had a dream— repeated three times. I fell into a sort of stupid state, without exactly being asleep, And three times I saw two persons—a man and a woman—quarrell- ing togetherin a dark place withwater flowing rapidly beneath. Itseenied inany dream that the quarrel referred to my brother, and once I heard my brother's voice calling loudly for me; then the man pushed the woman, and she fell, and I saw her struggling in the water. Wasn't it strange I should dream that three times? Now I know you will laugh at me." " No, I shall not laugh' " he said ; " but You must know as well as I do that these dreams and presenti- ments are all bosh, for one that conies right there are hundreds that come p 3 nothing." "But three times "The same causes operated each time on a suscep- tible temperament like yours,' lie answered quietly. "And yet there are some people who think that—. Chat our true relations to space are not exactly those we, suppose them to be when we are awake," he said as calmly. " But how will that help you to connect your dream with Raymond ?" " I arn somehow frightened about that woman." "Your imagination has invented the woman. There are ideas which people the air, and we imagine them to be realities. " Then you think there is nothing the matter ?" "Why Mould there be anything more than we know to be the matter f Bad" news travels fast enough." "Raymond has not written to me for more , than a

- . - month.' " tie would telegraph about the smallest thing fast enough, but it was alwaYs difficult to get him to write a decent letter." It was of no use. She was shaken and unstrung. "Somehow I am so nervous. I don't know how bear it," she said, appealing to him with those 410,va eyes $o difficult W withstand,

div.head: CHAPTER XXVIII.
div.p: CHAPTER XXVIII.
A LUSCIOUS BIT FOR SCANDAL MONGERS.

For the next ,day or two Ursula had not only to hear of the gossip, which, once set going, taxed the imagination to invent and add a thousand details, but she had also to put up with Dr. Havard's vehement abuse of the young Frenchman. If the doctor had known as much about women as he pretended, he might have guessed at the flow of honest indignation which would make Ursula take the part of a much abused man—an indignation which at this crisis she was almost ready to mis- takeforlove. Women are always violent partisans, and Ursula—like a child in her wilfulness, her pets and • humours—suddenly ceased over-quoting the sayings of the man whom she had hitherto delighted to honour, and devoted herself to Grandet. The doctor kept his own counsel, but Mrs. Wilsoll, who was continually saying that she was sure she was "not clever enough to be Miss Campion's companion," suddenly asserted herself a little. "Do you think it is quite wise to let that young Frenchman be so often here ?" "Quite I " said Ursula merrily, "I was certain he would turn up I" "Yo i know what ,they are saying ? " ventured the old lady rather nervously, referring to the luscious bib of scandal-mongering which had brought Dr. Havard in such haste to see his ward. "I should call it a piece of shabby desertion if I gave up an old friend because of what they are saying.' "Doesn't she mean to deny it Mrs. Wilson asked the doctor. . .

But even he put her off with some vague answer, ' in rather a moody manner. It seemed to :Ursula quite a piece of unnecessary Quixotism—of knight errantry which she could well have afforded to do without—when even Fielding shewed that he was nervous and excited on the subject. "She calls herself my friend--she pretends to be influenced by me, but she always treats me like a fool," her thought not unnaturally, when he saw her, so constantly associated with Grandet, "Oh, yes, she makes fools of us all very neatly I" He hadbecoms used to Ursula Campion's faults, to her little fits of anger; but that her aspirations, her theories, her observations on life, her conviction that she should remain single should all so suddenly have vanished, seemed to him inexplicable. It made lqin hard upon the Frenchman. It was horrible—insupport- ablehe could not bear to see them together. En- thusiastic as Ursula was, he had thought the country of her choice would be with "chosen souls," as Madame de Stied would have said; but that she— who did not seem likely to submit to the thraldom of married life, to whom all restraint was irksome— should bind herself to a man who had little noble to recommend him, was more than passing strange? What could have tempte4 her to break her resolution? He so far broke down in his own resolutions as to refer one day to the fact that "he could no longer expect her to give so much help" to his schemes, as when she was married she might have other purposes for her money." The tight strain which she had lately put on herself, and which seemed at times to be killing though it could not be relaxed, made her burst Into a laugh which was rather bitter as she answered-- "And who told you I was to be married? it is one thing to look seawards, and another to put to sea." "Then my information is incorrect? "he said, speaking in a stifled voice. "Is it fair to cross-examine me?" she asked, puzzling him by one of those appealing looks which seemed, as before, to crave approbation. "You have known me too short a time to have as right to ask such a question." He bowed, and would have left her. But her mood became suddenly softened. She put out a detaining hand— "lf—if I have a secret—it is a secret with which any girl might trust her mother." But it was he who was roused now, "You refer to the short time I have known you," he said, in a low voice, "may I remind you that some things are not to be measured by time?" In that moment the veil was lifted. She had a glimpse of the whole man; she had only seen the shadow of him before, Pe Oil bi u.ltic9 kti- ing that his passionate keeling for her had sifted IT- self clear from all littleness and meanness—all baser ' motive—money had nothing to do with his evident liking for her. And yet that liking made it hardet for her to persist in her resolution. " I should like to see my m3ther's portrait to- night,' she thought to herself that evening as she unlocked it from the drawer of relics in which she generally kept it. "I have a reason for it." And yet she scarcely acknowledged the reason to herself as she gazed at it like a heirless child, and longed for her mother. The next time she saw Fielding she- took him, as she had often done before, by surprise. "Please don't think any the less of me as a friend,* she said, with a vexed and impatient look on her speaking face, "if there are some things about my past life I can't possibly explain." All the hardness had gone out of her—she was soft and pptural i sp I"['lease don't think it is my fault," she continued, her Nice betruing a quaver. - And then, bolero he had time to cut the interview short, she added, as quickly— " What does it matter what people think, if my friends stißbelieve in me?'

-. The allusion to their friendship outraged him a little. He forgot for the moment that it was his own faultif he had not taken advantage of his opportunity; forgot alsa that this was a woman to whom repression was horrible, and to whom the consideration of con- ventionalities was unnatural. , "I wish I knew what was right," she said medita- tively—" what Christians would think right. I was not brought up to believe in Christianity, and yet sometimes I feel almost as if I do. Now, if you have made a promise—are you bound to keep it like an ' oh, when the circumstar-ces have changed—when ... 'Welt anything but Christian at that moment. He regroach nil himself afterwards for speaking brutally w en—to izhorten the agony he was suffering— he interrupted iir,and said— .:: " You honoured nu: once before by asking for my advice, but, if I remembea. rightly, you had no idea of taking it. I have learnt .to give more than is ab- nen; solntely necessary." . . "Oh yes, I remember, you s,lici ,-;mething about z grand ladies driving down in their. o,rriages and making a sort of luxury of visiting or foi4s in the East-end, and then coming back to their ,putple and fine linen, just as if you thought they must 9njoy it by contra 4" ' 1 _ . _ _ _ - -- - -

SOmehow this account of his words did pot sound sympathetic, but he did not say, "You wrong me ! " In the subtleties of thought which rushed through ,his brain—in the receptivity of the man—a terribly momentous possibility was present to his mind, and he felt that if lie wbuld do his duty, it was quick sympathy he had to be on his guard against, and it ?Jaz safer to seem cold. He need not have feared that he would have to listen to the confidences of a love-sick girl. The moanings would, apparently, be all of another kind. She was too much in earnest, too absorbed in her own difficulty to give way to shy secrecy any more. Again, the veil had been raised,. and spirit for the instant met spirit. She stood re- vealed as she really was, her face clouded with pain, a sort of mist 'before her eyes, her teeth set, appeal. big to him for help with a sort of cry of which, as a man of honour, he cou'd not possibly take advantage. "Did I say that?" he answered, in a tone which sounded to her ears like one of lofty irritation, bid in which he scarcely recognised his own voice. "I at afraid I must have seemed to give hard advice then, and must give hard advice now. A promise is a promise—l fail to see how you can break it." He turned away as he uttered the last words, and she did not see the look in his own dark grey, deepset eyeswhich might otherwise have frightened her. He had given the verdict she expected, and she had no- thing now to do but to try her best to be good to the other friend who had cared for her when she had led the old hard life in Paris. After all, as she told her- self, she owed Grandet much. It was he who had invested the most of his treasure in her happines.l when others had invested so little. .He had loved her before she had been credited with the possession'of money. Latterly she hacl been cold as ice to Louis Grandet, and he had decided that Englishwomen had no hearts.
" A paragon---one always hates those models of perfection—she is,growing dull, flat, and unin- teresting," the young Frenchman had said to him- self.

She had indeed tried his patience to the uttermost, and appeared to the least ad-vantage when he intruded upon her, without, she declared, saying so much " byyour leave." Her brilliant eyes had, expanded,

• Had he Snot always heard that the ng called "love" had its surprises breaking thre—gh all pre- conceived designs, sweeping away all logic, defying all calculation? It was said to seize you as the spirit of prophecy seized the Pythoness, pronouncing words Which you had not intended—betraying your secrets. Some such impulse he felt, and was on his guard against the danger. The sublime folly said to raise and transfigure a man—to,make a vulgar man a poet, and a coward a hero—could also make a noble man mean, and change a hero into a coward. - The appealing face looked heavy with anxiety now that the tears were dried. But he quickly looked away. "I don't think you have any reason to apprehend worse than I have told you. I blame myself now for what I told you." "No, you were quite right to tell me the truth. I should not expect you to soften it. Why should you try to, soften anything ? " she said with sudden passion. 41 Are we not friends—always Mends? Will you not always continue to speak the truth to me?" _ _

The words recurred to his memory— 'So live we then, nor heed what whisper tells, That closest union heaviest reckoning pays; In shock of loss and anguish of farewells. In the eternal parting of the ways." "Yes, we are friends," he answered, 14 he rose to go. "And you will take a friend's advice and not think so excitedly about this." They did not say a single word more to each other, but it was as if a new compact had taken place between them. The strange anxious look had passed from her face; but that very night the Eumenides, which had been waiting behind the closed door, Sprang out upon her. • It was in the form of.e, telegram, from one of the young artists whom she had formerly known as a student at the Atelier Desnoyers : "Come, or send assistance, at once. A terrible tragedy has 'taken place here, and your brother is implicated in it."
(To be continued.)
CHRISTMAS AT WARRINGTON.

The grand old Christmas festival has this year been kept up in Warrington with even more than usual fervour, and although the weather has been inclement and unseasonable, public enjoyment seemed general both outside and in. 'Poorer people were not forgotten, for besides the dinner given by the Mayor to all comers, many private individuals added to the comfort and enjoyment of those to whom both were limited. At the Workhouse and at the Padgate Industrial Schools, inmates and scholars, besides the usual Christmas "spread," were entertained with music, singing, &c., afterwards,and on the Boxing Day, they were taken to a special per- formance at the Public Hall of "My Sweetheart," which it is needless to say was heartily appreciated by them. Bands of music and carol singers were more numerous than ever on Christmas Day and on the evening before. The interior of the churches were, as usual, decorated with flowers and "evergreens., At the Parish Church, the decora- tions were of a more elaborate character than has been seen for some years. A beautiful white cross, made of Christmas roses, camellias, hyacinths, and maidenhair fern, the gift of Lady Lilford, which was placed above the altar, was especially notice- able. The decorations of St. Paul's and Holy Trinity Churches, though not; so extensive, were very pretty in general effect. St. James', Latch- ford, and St. Anne's, Winwick-street, were also seasonably adorned. The schoolroom in John- street, which at present serves as St. Peter's Church, was also embellished with holly, misletoe, &c., a. lack of quantity being made up for by the taste with which the decorations were arranged. St. Barnabas Church was also noticeable for some tasteful decorations. At the Roman Catholic Churches Christmas, was celebrated, as usual, with much solemnity. Each priest offered up three masses, this being the only day in the whole year in which he can do so. At eleven o'clock the grandest ceremony of Oh Catholic Church began, namely, solemn high mass. The interior of St. Al ary's Buttermarket-street, had been tastefully decorated. The chief attraction was the crib, or representation of the Saviour's birth at Bethlehem, which it erected in one of the side chapels. It is made to represent a cavern stable by the hill side. In the interior of the stable the figure of the infant Saviotir can be seen lying on straw in the centre, on one side being the figure of St. Joseph, and on the other the figure of Mary, his mother, kneeling as if in adoration. The statues are about life size, and look very natural. There is an opening at „ the back 'A the efive;aS'i the hellole of the OX and the fig are shown, and look as if about to enter. Still further at the back is a scene 6h ettlith. side of Bethlehem. The interior of the cave is illuminated with gas jets, and the outside is covered with evergreens. The star of Bethlehem is arranged in a lamp, and placed above the cave, I Tbe picture is a touching as well as an appropriate and beautiiul one, and is viewed by large numbers of people. At the St. Albans, Bewsey-st., the . church was also decorated with evergreens. The music at the High Mass was of ti very attractive character, the fine choir being assisted by an orchestral band, which consisted of some of the best players in this district. The music selected was Mozart's "Twelfth Mass," which was rendered with &eat effect. At the conclusion of the Mass, the choir and orchestra gave the chorus, Arid the glory of the Lord," from the "Messiah." Some of the Sunday schools also gave treats to their young people, and among young and old no one appears to have this year been forgotten in the fun and \ feasting. Wednesday was also very generally regarded as a holiday by shopkeepers and work- people. Among the amusements of the day were two football matches on the Wilderspool ground which were witnessed by large gatherings of spectators; and in the evening, the play of "My Sweetheart" at the Public Hall was enjoyed by crowded house.

THE REV. JOHN VONGE ON CHRISTMAS FEASTING. The Rev. John Yonge pastor of Wycliffe Congre- gational Church, Warrington, preached on Sunday evening to a large congregation from the words "Whether therefore ye eat or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God," which he gave as a Christmas motto for everyone." In the course of his sermon Mr. Yonge said :'—The precept of this text presents itself at a season like this with a considerable 'degree of peculiar timeliness. This season of the year is one of general festivity. Those who do not keep the feast of Christmas keep the feast of New Year, and very many keep both. Even the larger multitude, whq CM; little or 110tbir” abont the Lel'^inns origin or character of diristrna§Reicing, seize the =amen sO prOVided for all kinds of MirthfUl, and somethne§almost mad, festivi- ties. The fact that " Christina§ Corms but once a year" is held by them to demand ace to justify all sorts of feasting, all degrees of frivolous gaiety; all manner of exciting amusement. It is a melancholy and shameful fact that the season which celebrates the advent of the world's Redeemer, the purpose of whose mission Was to deliver Men from the curse and power of sin, is con- sidered by large numbers of people to be fitly commemor- ated, not only by unusual and of;en immoderate eating, but by still more immoderate and intemperate drinking. It was once Stated by an eminent authority that at the time of Christmas and New Year in Loselon there was vastly more illness produced by the immoderate and intemperate celebration of the season by the people who had money than by the meagre fare and even almost starvation state of the poverty stricken., There seems to be almost a stubborn prejudice in many minds against moderate habits at Christmas. It is too generally regarded as the time to launch out in food, drink, dress, gaiety, excitement ; and some there are who seem to be of opinion that even a measure of actual excess is at least excutable at such a season. Magistrates and police are said to be specially lenient at such a season. The police do not too readily "see" cases of disorder, and knagistrate,s deal tenderly in honour of the season! A circumstance has recently occurred connected with Christmas festivity in Warrington upon which it is desirable to speak an earnest word of protest. The Guardians of the Poor for this town, notwithstanding a serious illustration last Christmas of the unwisdom of their policy, have again granted the inmates of the house a special allowance of intoxicating' drink as a necessary celebration of the birth of Jesus Christ. I venture to dissent from and strongly disapprove of this repeated act of unwisdom. No one could wish other than that they who are so unfortunate as to have only the poor house for their home should enjoy as many, com- forts and pleasures at this season as an properly be provided. But, in view of the unquestioned fact that most of the icmates of our workhouses owe their presence there to the evils of intemperance, it does seem a strange and incongruous idea that they should cele- brate Christmas by special indulgence in the very thing which has helped to their misfortune. This is a way of Christmas rejoicing which cannot commend itself to any serious and thoughtful mind It should be the endeavour of Christian people to moderate and amend the popular idea and habit of Christmas festivity. It can be done in good measure by the force of persistent and consistent example. It can be done in further measure by the gradual creation of a letter public opinion. Let it come to be understood that the season of Christmas is far from being a warrantable excuse for lack of modera- tion, the relaxation of the righteous rules of ordinary , life; that it is as indecorous and evil to cross the boun- daries of sobriety and good behaviour at this season as at any other; that the frequent spectacle of intemper- ance, such as will be seen in special degree in the streets

of our town at this season, is no occasion for smiles and and laughter, but rather for sorrow and shame. That a celebration of Christmas, whether in the privacy of houses or the publicity of assemblies, institutions, and places of general resort, which consists largely in what leads to "excess Of riot," is an insult to high }leaven, a mockery and a grief to Him who came to save mankind from sin.

HOT-POTS FOR THE POOR.. Following out the usual custom in Warrington, the Mayor (Alderman T. H. Sutton), entertained the poor to a het-pot "dinner on Christmas Day. The meal ,was served in the Drill Hall, and over 600 needy people availed themselves of the invitation of

his lit &still), and brought appetites of surprising vigour to bear on the hot-pots, which were served in small tin dishes. Mr. George Riley, the school attendance officer, undertook the task of distribut- ing the tickets, and superintending matters at the Drill Hall when the feast came off. The first comers were served at noon, and for an hour •ifterwards the scene was a very busy one, a staff of voluntary waiters being kept busy attending to the wants of the guests, who were continually handing up their dishes for another, and yet another, supply of the appetising fare. That the guests enjoyed the meal was evident from their satisfied and complacent appearance when they left the Hall. Those who came ragged. shivering, and miserable, left smiling and happy, though ragged still, and before leaving theyleartily cheered the donor of the treat. The following ladies and gentlemen, amongst others, assisted in attending to the wants of the guests :—Mrs. Wilkinson, the Misses Allton, the Misses Geddes, the Misses Chrimes, Miss Shaw Green, Miss M. JsaaP, Rev. S. Wilkinson, Rev. T. Emmett, Mr. and Mrs. Macgilevary, Councillor J. Shaw Green, Councillor Wm. Tinsley, Councillor J. E. Wright, Councillor Thomas Jolley, Mr. Thomas Morris, Mr. Thomas Domville, Mr. John Griffiths, Mr. Thomas Cox, Mr. George Woods, Mr. James Smethurst, Mr. George Anton, Mr. Edward Green, and Mr. H. Cookson. Amongst others present were the Mayor (Alderman Sutton),- Mrs. Willis, Mrs. Harrison, Mrs. Francottb, Mrs. Carleton, Mrs. Venn, Mrs. Thomas Morriir, Mrs. Massey, Miss Atkinson, Rev. J. Hands, Lieutenant-Colonel Bolton, Alderman Harrison, Councillor Francomb, Mr. William Sharp, Mr. G. Griffiths,Mr. Wm. Reid, and Mr. Win. Burgess. Towards the conclusion of the repast the choir boys irorn St. Paul's Church sang an appropriate selection. The Mayor addressed a few words to the recipi- ents of his bounty. He expressed the pleasure he felt at seeing so many of the Warrington poor there that day, and hoped they had enjeyed their Christmas dinner. Christmas, he said, was a time of rejoicing a time when all expected to have a good dinner and enjoy themselves. (Applause.) He did not think there were quite so may guests present this year as last year, and he was pleased to think that that was an indication of better times, and that there was more work and not so much distress in the town. (Applause.) He was very glad to find that that was the case, because everybody in the town would enjoy a much happier Christmas when they knew there was not so much destitution. He had to thank Mr. Thomas Morris, Mr. Daniel Jones, and a good many other friends, Mr. Riley in particular, for their assistance. One and all he wished the company a ",Merry Christmas and a happy New Year." (Applause.) The Rev. S. Wilkinson, in moving a vote of thanks to the Mayor for his hospitality, remarked that it had been

the cuslom now for some years for the Mayor of the borough to entertain his poorer brethren on Christmas morning, and he was quite sine Alderman Sutton would enjoy his own dinner all the more with the knowledge that he had already satisfied the appetites of that gather- ing. (Applause.) He trusted that Alderman Sutton would have a very happy and successful year, as Mayor, and that next year a similar company would be found seated at those tables. (Applause.) Hearty cheers were then given for his Worship, after which the com- pany dispersed. Before leaving, however, the children were supplied with oranges, and the old men with small packetsa tobacco. Mrs. Booth superintended the cook- ing arrangements, and it may be added that in making the hot pots 2cwt. 16Ibs. of beef and mutton, 311 cwt. of potatoes, and 601 b. of onions were used. AT THE WORKHOUSE. '

The customary substantial treat was given to the inmates of the Workhouse on Christmas day. The large dining hall, in which the dinner was served, was very agreeably decorated with holly and other evergreens, Chinese lanterns, &c. The dinner con- sisted of roast beef and plum pudding with the usual accessories, and also included a pint of beer to those male inmates, who desired it and half-a- pint each to the females, coffee being given to the children and thoee of the elders who did not take beer. Amongst those present in the course of the dinner were his Worship the Mayor (Alderman Sutton), Mr. and Mrs. Thomas Morris, Miss Woods, Mrs. and Miss Blackhurst ; Messrs. Thomas Jolley, Robert leherweod, Thomas Jones, and James Strange and (*. He wished them all "A Merry Christmas and a happy New Year:" (Applause.) At a 'at stage, the Master called upon the inmates to accord a hearty vote of thanks to the Guardians for their kind- ness in providing them with such an excellent meal. (Applause.) They had done so with great heartiness, mid it had been arranged that during the afternoon tobacco and snuff should be given to those inmates who cared for these things. (Applause.) He hoped they would enjoy themselves in a reasonable and proper manner, and not let the beer g!t into their heads. (An inmate "I don't think a pint of beer will hurt any- ono."—Laughter and applause.) He called upon them to give three hearty cheers for the Guardians. This request was complied with very heartily. Mr. Isherwood (who had assisted Mr. and Mrs. Ward and the other officials in waiting upon the inmates) returned thanks on behalf of the Guardians. The Guardians, he said, did not think any harm was being done in even giving them a pint of beer, but it must be understood that everyone had his views with regard to the beer question. They must understand that when he objected to the supplying of beer he was not ashamed to say so. He did not drink beer himself, and had never done so. He was very pleased to see them enjoy themselves, and he did not begrudge the little services he had been able to render that day to add to their pleasurd and comfort. (Applause.) IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
1100S1, COMINIONS.--SATunDAy. THE PARNELL COMISSION.

A sharp discuson arose upona motion by Mr. Km- nxn. The hon. gentleman in'the first instance sat Close to the Speakei?s chair and 'read something which was absolutely unintelligible to 'Oro House. He was chal- lenged by M. Sexton to -speak up, and he then pro- ceeded to .a place below the gangway and presented a petition from Messrs. Sormnes, the solicitors for The Times, praying that the proper officer of the House might attend the Special Commission, in order to produce the test roll'frotn the yeareitTs to 1888. Objection was taken to the proceeding by Mr. Ssrron, who suggested that It would have been proper that notice df the 'petition should have been given to Mr. Yarnell, Whereupon the Sessxxn explained that application was made) to him during the adjournment for the productimref the roll, and ho consented, on the condition that all parties interested should have access tett. 'Afterwards he thought it well that a formal peti- tion should be presented to the House.—Mr. SEXTON intimated that he must challengs a division, and the House dividodoVith the result that the motion was car- ried by 54 votes to 13. The minority of 13 included Messrs.'Carew, Cox, Pickensgill, H. Lawson, G. B. Clark, Howell, Mc. Rwan, Graham, and S. Stevenson, and Sir .'Cleo.`CamPl3Bl. LATE SITTINGS.

'Sir MrDAL •RongirrsoN addressed a question to Mr. llosnhen, sifting whether the Government could giv.e any undertaking that the House should not in the future sit later than one o'clock in the morning.—Mr. Goscrrint expresstid his sensibility of the sacrifices which members haii'made' in attending the late sittings of the House during the past few weeks, but pointed out that it was impossible to make any definite promise that should limit' ths hours of sitting, which must necessarily he extended towards the close of the Session. 'PARLIAMENTARY REPORTING.
Mr. 'JAcirsom announced that the contract for Parlia- mentary reporting had nas.ed into the hands of Messrs. 'Macrae, of' London, who would do the work without subsidy. THE FIGHTING AT SUAKIN!.

'Mr; Costarax informed the Rouse that no further news had been received by the Government concerning Stan- 'ley and Emin Bev, and further that the accounts of the rmtnber of casualties in the battle at Suakim were so 'far as they knew corect. Mr. CREM/iII described the action as a battle of the Arabs; for the use of which expression he was called to order. and Mr. GoscitaK characterised the term, amid -some Cheering, as an insult to the British troops.

THE POST OFFICE SAVINGS BANK. ' On the motion for the third reading of the Appropria- tion Bill, Mr. liowxtr. called attention to certain regnla- tions which had recently come into force affecting the deposit of the moneys of Friendly Societies in the Post- office Sayings Bank, whereby the notice of withdrawal must .be signed by the whole of the trristees.—Mr. JecxsoN offered to give attention to the matter, and the subject was not further pursued. A discussion was then initiated by Mr. C. GrIARAN with respect t the condition of Cradley Heal] nail makers and the Bar' 'on gunlock filers, in the course of which Mr. STLVEI.I IILT, expressed the opinion that the trade at Darlaston had decayed so rapidly that &forte should be made to introduce a new ind"ustry there.—Mr. Rrrcrag pointed out how difficult it was to legislate for distress of this kind, but assured the House that the matter was haying, and should centlinue to have, his anxious consideration. Mr. Gasman replied to the varions ,qcestions which had been raised, and at 4 30 the House carried the third reading of the bill without a division. A few moments afterwards the House adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS.--MONDAY.-

The H;t;is—e—of-Eor—ds met ephortty after noon, when the. 'Royal assent VMS given by cominim;on to several bills, including the Consolidated Fund, Appropriation, Oaths, Liability of Trustees, Crofters lioldinfrs, Solicitors, and Libel Law Amendment Acts. Several :ladies took seats on the Peers' benches, but only threel.ords were present in addition to the Commissioners.

The Speaker of the House of C4mraone -and several members attended at the bar. THE QUEEN'S SPEECH. The Queen's Speech was read as follows: My LORDS AND ORNTLENVN,—I have great satisfac- tion in being able to release you from ..your protracted labours. . .
My relations with all Foreign Powens ontinue to be friendly. _ _

I regret that the Convention whit.% was concluded between myself and the President of the'U.S.. for the adjustment of the questions which 'had Arisen in refer- once to the fisheries in North AmericAn waters, has not commended itself to the judgment of the Senate of the United States, in whom, 11 ecording to the constitution of that country, the power of the ratification is vested. The temporary arrangements, howeverovirich have been adopted will, I trust, prevent any immediate inconveni. ence.arising from this decision. The conference which has been highl.ore the subject of bounties upon the exportation of sugars s been brought .to a satisfactory issue by the conclusion-of a convention for their abolition, which has been eigned by the repre- sentatives of most of the sugar producing countrles. _ . . .

_ The restoration of Egypt to a 'condition-a political and financial security has been for the timeinterrupted by an attempt on the part of the Soudaces() to possess theinselves of the port of Suakim. The dispersion of the besieging forces has been effected'hy-s.tbrilliant mili- tary operation on the part of the F.gyptien troops, sup- vorted h n British contingent In ethevrespects, the administrative and economical pravess oof Egypt has been sat is fac iory. An insurrection has broken out upon -tioc continenthl portion of the dominions of the P,ttitatt of --Zanzibar, which has brought with it considerable destraction of life and property in the German settlemetrrts on , that coast It, is evident that the renewed vigour of the have trade of which symptoms have unhappily hown- themselves in several parts-of Africa, has largely contribt.rted to the production of -these disturbances, I haw joined with the Emperor of Germany in estghlishirg,v. a [MVO blockade of that,part of the coast which is irr-insurrec- tion, in order to prevent not only the eccportation of slaves, but also the importation of munitions of -war.

My Indian dominions have enjoyed geperAl tran- quillity and prosperity during the past year. ;Thsturb- ances, however, hive occurred in the neiga,euring region of the Blacktlountains and on the extremo Iron- M,...er of Sikkim, butit.:ley havo been terminateddwithout ittfficulty. . . . . .

A rebellion which,4l,toke out in Afeleanistau ~under ishak Khan, and whie:n at one time threatened 10-eaGll tne .iortuidable proportioty-, has been entirely subdued by the military forces of te:e A meer. ‘A rising on the part C. some Zulu chiefs, which ,does not seem to have met sui:.ll any sympathy on tnepett of the:population, has beer, zuppressed by my troops,and tbemative levies and chiefs concerned in it areewait,ing trial before a special connaission. 110 USE OF COMMUM..—Mowns.r. trwenty-tw,o members, including Mr. Speaker, cams Sawn 'to the House, in the afterfi.im, to transact what little business was on the paper, api to assist at th€ prorogation. 11r. Parnell was in t. 1.1.0 House early to inspect the test roll of members at the table of the Bowe.

At a quarter ,past 12 Black Rod wen:announced, and requested the atteinds.nce of the C01111114411S in the House of Peers to hear the Commission read. Iwo score mem- bers passed through the lobbies to theklpper Chamber, returning 20 minutes later, when the Speaker immedi- ately rea the tQuesn's Speech on the prorNation of Parliatuvot. Commencing with Mr. Murficlla, the soli- tary representative cC the front Oppositica bench in attendance, all the Members present passed around the table and toak leave of the Speaker. At minutes to one the Speaker aelt, the Rouse, and the .session of 1888 was brought to.an,and. Parliament was prorogded until the 31st int.

TIM BAPTIST VP•von.—Ve year's statistics of the Bap- tist Union of Great Nita*, and Tre,and have beau pub- lished. Special interest attaches to the question of increase or decrease in the numerical strength of the AenoMiaation in Vi6W a the recent down grade reon- troveray. The returns giuoa are as follows :--2,170 clx.lrches, 3,745 chapels, 1;221ig23 chapel seats, 292.418 members, 45,977 Sunday sehool teachers, 452,1.0 scholars, 3.938 local preachers, and 1,865 pastors in charge. These figures show when compared with /est yeas an increase of six churches, 44 chapels, 23,7943 chapel seats, a decrease of 4,887 members, 809 Sunday school teachers, 6,033 scholars, 180 local preachers, and an increase of five pastors in charge. However, some of the larger churches which furnished returns for 1887 have not done so for 1883, and in considaration of these, as well as a considerable number of churches which never send returns, an addition of about 25,000 mem- bers and 30,000 scholars should, it is estimated, be made 1 to the above figures. A shocking attempt at murder and suicide was made on Saturday afternoon at Leicester. A man named Middleton, a plumber by trade, in a fit of jealousy attacked his wife with a hammer, inflicting severe in- juries about the head. A neighbour hearing screams entered the house, and found the woman in a pool of blood and unconscious. while police were being sum. moned Middleton cut his throat with a clasp knife. Both were removed to the Infirmary. The woman is in a' critical state, but Middleton's wound is only superficial. The parties have nine children.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 29, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 29, 1888.

BANK QUAY MISSION, WARRINGTON. MR. JOHN CROSFIELD ON HIS TRAVELS: The annual tea party in connection with the Bank Quay Workingmen's Mission was held, on Wednes- day evening, when about 200 people sat down to tea, and attended a subsequent meeting. Advan- tage was taken of the occasion to make interesting presentations to Mr. and Mrs. John Crosfield, on , their return from their wedding tour, the teachers and scholars deeming the opportunity given them .of testifying their esteem and respect for Mr.aind 'Mrs. Croalleld a very suitable one. The presents. took the shape of a Wesleyan Hymn Bonk, with O tunes, and a revised version of the Bible. n the- front page of the hymn book was the following inscription:—"Presented to Mr. and Mrs. John Crosfield, from the teachers and scholars of the Workingmen's Mission. Warrington, December 20th,1 1888." The inscription on the Bible read :—"This revised version of the Holy Bible, with the Wes- leyan Hymn and Tune Book, was given to Mr. and Mrs. John Crosfield, on the occasion of their marriage, by the teachers and scholars of the Workingmen's Mission Sabbath School, with , the sincere prayer that the blessino. of God may con- stantly attend them." The volumes, it may be added, were handsomely bound, and the inscriptions had• been most admirably done by Mr. Frank Williams. Mr. Croefleld is the founder of both tilt school and chapel, and a treat is annually given to the scholars, at which Mr. Crosfield always endea- vours to attend. This year, in consequence of the increasing popularity of the celebration, it was , decided to occupy two evenings. On Wednesday the senior scholars had their treat, and the juniors had their turn on the following evening. The school, as will be gathered from particulars given in the annual report, is in a very flourishing condition. On entering the room, Mr. and Mrs. Crosfield, who were accompanied by Miss E. and Master G. Crosfield, were greeted with much cheering. Mr. Crosfield I occupied the chair. After the meeting had com- menced with singing and prayer, Mr. R. Tasurnn, the secretary, read the annual report. It stated that during the year they had lost three of the scholars through death. In con- nection with the school there was a Band of Hope, and it was believed that when arrangements now in hand were completed they would be able to extend their usefulness in that direction. There was also a Mutual Improvement Society, and the session had been a very pleasant and instructive one. They felt assured that, under the able presi- dency of Mr. John Dawber, the school would continue to prosper. There had recently been additions to the library. The choir, in addition to the duties that devolved upon them in connection with their own church, had given generous help to other institutions in the town, notably to the Mission on the Acton Grange section of the Man- chester Ship Canal. The numbers of teaehers on the books were :—females 7, males 17, total 24; aver- age morning attendance, females 3, males 10, total 13; average afternoon attendance, females 6, males 16, total 22. The number of scholars upon the books was 550. The average attendance in the morning was—females 63, males 95 ; and in the afternoon—females 173, and males 188. The officers for the coming year were,—president, Mr. Joseph Monks, sen.; superintendents, Messrs. John Dawber and Thomas Taylor.; secretary, Mr. R.. E. Tanner; treasurer, Mr. James Woolley; visitors, Messrs. Joseph Monks, sen., and Richard William- son; librarian, Mr. Frank Williams, and assistant, Mr. Henry Kay. The accounts showed a small balance in hand. Mr. CROSTIELD, who was received with cheers, said We quite intended to be here at half-past seven, but my old friend, and companion in my travels last year, Alderman Joseph Davies—whom, I think, everyone in this room knows—came to see me this evening, and our meeting was so cordial that I could not separate from him. (Applause.) I am very pleased to hear such a favourable report as the one read by the secretary, and it is very gratifying to me to know that there are 500 children in this part of Warrington who are on the books of this Sunday schOol, and that you have an attendance here, on an average, on Sunday afternoons, of some 350 children. There must be an amount of good done by this school that it is impossible for me, or for anyone else, to estimate, because we none of us can tell what seeds are being sown, and what harvest may be gathered. There is no doubt whatever in my mind, or in the mind of any sensible man or woman, that whatever child attends this Sunday school on a Sunday afternoon, or a Sunday morning, must be better than if that child was left to ramble about the streets uncared for and unnoticed. It is, I believe,about 'fifteen years since the commencement of this school, and it began, as some of you may know, in a small room on the other side of the road, in a fustian cutting shop, with. I believe, about six children. It has grown -steadily year by year, until this building has certainly got.as many children as it can hold. I want to repeat here, -what! think I say almost every Christmas, that you children, and you parents, ought never to for- get the debt that you owe to the teachers ef this School. Remember that they devote every Sunday to the teaching of these children,without any reward, except that reward tuthich iis of more value than any money— the reward of doing their duty. (Applause.) I must impress upon the parents the necessity and import- ance of seeing that their children attend this school regularly, because I know from my own experience how hopeless it is to influence properly the mind of a child, without you-can have regular attendance. It is snly fair to the teachers, it is only right, that the Parents should see that their children do not neglect going to the Sunday School, provided that they are in good health. Of course, if it is a case of Sickness, it cannot be helped. since I last saw you I have just returned home from a very delightful trip of nearly three months in Italy, and I would like to tell you children a little of what we saw whilst we were in that beautiful country. I cannot tell you much., because of the time it would take, but I want to tell you that we went through the most beauti- ful scenery in the Italian Lakes, where we had blue skies and a het sun, and it was so hot that we were LORD ROSERERY AT AIRDRIE. glad to get under the shelter of the trees to be out of Lord Roseber.v, addressing a demonstration at Airdrie, the sunshine. div.head: MR. GLADSTONF, AT NAPLES,
div.p: MR. GLADSTONF, AT NAPLES,

Mr. Gladstone, on arriving at 2,lales on Saturday night, met with a most warm and enthusiastic recep- tion. The vestibule of the station was crowded with students in many-coloured caps, who bore with them the llniversity flag. Shortly before ten the red lights of the approaching engine were seen, and vociferous cheers greeted the arrival of the train, which passed along the platform to its extreme end. As it did so, a medical student sprang on to the step of the carriage, where Mr. Gladstone's venerable head was seen, as, leaning ont of the window, hat in hand, he responded to the greet- ings of those present. Ile was addressed by the student, who in the name of his *xatipanions -welcomed the illus- trious statesman as the friend of Italy and the writer of the celebrated letters 'which contributed so largely 'to the redemption of Italy. Shouts of "Viva Gladstone," "Viva Ireland," arr.d. "Viva England," greeted this speech, to which Mr. Gladstone replied that after 38 years' absence from Naples he we greatly touched at the enthusiaside reception accorded to him by its authorities and' its students, for whom he had always entertained a warm affection. He took thieopportunity of thanking them for the address sent him in commemora- tion of the tenth anniversary of Victor Emanuel's death, wad for the album presented to him at Florence. He could not better respond to their affectionate reception than by saying, "Viva Napoli ! Viva Italia!" Great cheering followed, and then Comtnendatore Morelli entered the carriage to greet Mr. Gladstone, who, on alighting, gave his arm to Mrs. Gladstone, and taking that of Signor Pallino passed to his carriage, which was surrounded by students with lighted 'torches. They ;visited to take out the horses, but this Mr. Gladstone would not permit. Mr. Gladstone, who looked exceed- ingly well, attended Divine service on Sunday morning, accompanied by Mrs. Gladstone and Mrs. Drew.

TILE LAND COURT MANIFESTO.

The Freemares Journal says theorder of the-Land Corn- missien not only blasts the hopes of thousands 'of Irish tenants, but.distinctly menaces the peace of the country, and .cannot fail to have the most unhappy results upon The Winter's tranquility. It is an official scandal, after a harvest much below the average, with a rise practi- cally only in cattle. llessrs.'Wrench and Pilton decree a series of Parliamentary reductionaf or the years from 1881 to 1884, but in many cases order an increase in the judicial rents for 1885. 'Never has a public depart- ment struCk .so far-reaching a, blow at public confidence and public peace, meant to bury the cry against arrears, and to give a fillip to Lord Ash- bourne's Act. But how long,will it last, and what will be the fate of'the illusions raised by this new rack-rent .manifesto? THE 'TENANTS' CRUSADE IN IRELAND.

The Freeman's Journal, in an article on the tenants' crusade in Ireland, says The hand has been put to the plough, and there can be no going back. There is some fresh developmentalmost every week, and it may possibly be, in view of the action of some of the Land Commissioners,' that, as Mr. Dillon says, a time will shortly come when the policy of keeping out of the 1.1,nd Courts until those tribunals come back to reason ,nay have to be adopted. 'lt is only by consolidating their organisation, and by uniting with discipline and iromrosolution, that the tenants will be ready for duty whenever therall is made to them. If they had nothing else to inspire them and cheer them on than the untiring md self-sacrificing, energy and Crusader-like courage of Mr. Dillon and Mr. O'Brien, they ought not to lack those attributes in abundance which command success."

Cohen, Q.C. (West Southwark), Mr. Lacaita (Dundee). Mr. Walter Shirley (Doncaster), Mr. W. .1. Evelyn (Deptford), the Earl of March (Chi- chester), Mr. C. H. James (Merthyr Tydvil). Mr. H. J. Lord Knuteford (Sir H. Holland) and the Duke of Rutland (Lord John Manners) vacated their seats in the Commons in eonsequence et becoming peers. The relative strength of the various political parties in the House of Commons has undergone very little change since the commencement of the year. The Liberal Unionists have lost a seat to the Gladstonians at Edinburgh, and another at Ayr, and have won one at Doncaster. The Conservatives have lost a seat at Southampton, and had no compensating gain. The net result is, therefore, that the Liberal Unionists and Conservatives are each weaker by one man than at the ecimmencement of the session, whilst the Gladstonians are stronger by two, counting four votes on a division.
