div.head: LORD 'RICNDOLPH CHURCHILL.
div.p: LORD 'RICNDOLPH CHURCHILL.

Lord Randolph ,Churchill has addressed the following letter to the chairman of the East Aberdeenshire Con- servative AssoCiation-!--," Many considerations, with which I will not trouble you, prevent me from accepting the kind and Lettering request that I should personally contest the constituency. 'I have very: strong • opinions that Scottish constituencies greatly prefer as their Par- liamentary representatives •men of Scottish birth and residence, and the tnionist•cause in East Aberdeenshire ought by no EIVAIIB to deprive itself of the advantages which a candidate with ,those qualifications ‘would possess."

Peter's, for the paintings have been removed to the Vatican, and they have got mosaic work to represent the pictures. Not one of you could tell, if you looked at those pictures, that they werenot the original paintings, because they are so beautifully done in stone. Mosaic work means this—some of you boys, perhaps, may know—small pieces of stone of different colours are put together to represent a picture. One of these pictures would be, I daresay, fifteen feet high and twelve feet broad, and I suppose that a picture like that, if done byl one man, would take at least a hundred years to make it. We saw them making those pictures, and we saw a comparatively small picture that a man was making, and they told us it would take that man thirty years to make it. They have 20,000 different coloured stones in the Vatican to make these pictures with They require every shade of colour. We went and saw the Coliseum, which you may have heard of. It was the scene centuries ago of the most awful brutality that the world over witnessed, and there men professing Chris- tianity were torn to pieces by wild boasts for the gratifi- cation of the Roman Enaperors. There stands the Coliseum still—an enormous ruin. The outside walls are 150 feet high ; and the building was capable of holding 100,000 people. There are stones in that building of a size that would perfectly astonishyou,and how they ever got them up passes man's comprehension now, with the means that they thenhad. So we went on and saw the different sights. We came to a new church called St. Paul's—the most gorgeous and richest church in Italy, with solid granite columns 60 feet high, and six feet in diameter. They were brought three or four hundred miles to adorn this chuich. The cost of bringing one of those columns is almost incalculable. Round the top of this building there are a number of portraits of the Popes, 250 of them, done in this mosaic work, and you may have an idea of the labour that has been spent upon the making of those portraits. The body of St. Paul is in this church, and no one is allowed to officiate at the Mass except the Pope himself. He is the only one considered suitable. We had the pleasure of meeting my old and dear friend Mr. William Davies, Mr. Robert Davies's brother. He lives in Rome, and we spent a most delightful Sunday with him visiting the ruins of the palace of the Caesars. The ruins are enormous. Of course, the roof and the walls are all gone, but the foundations are there, standing about three or four feet abode the ground. There are the banqueting room, and the sleeping reoms, while the frescoes painted on the walls, as fresh as if they were done yesterday, are 2,000 years old. We wandered about for two hours, and then, to my 'astonishment, we got to the edge of it, looking down on to the Forum and the Capitol, and we found that the whole time we had been walking about forty feet above the level of the ground, and there was arch upon arch below our feet/ There was this immense pile, covering as much as a spi-acre field, I should think, and it was all arches underneath. From there we went to Naples. We saw Vesuvius; and he was smoking away—(laughter) —and was turning out a cloud of smoke—more than Dallam forge and the White Cross works put together— a great black cloud in the sky that you could see for twenty miles. At night the appearance was that of a huge bonfire. There were plenty of visitors going up Vesuvius when we were there. I went up the mountain thirty years ago and I did not care to trouble the old fellow again. it the top of the mountain yon find bits of pure sulphur, and the smoke that comes out more resembles cotton wool than anything else. We gave one of the waiters two penny pieces to put into the red hot lava at the top. He did so, and brought a penny piece back, when it had gone cold, in his pocket. I have given it to my little girl, and she has it at home. It is apiece of lava with a penny piece in it. We then went to Sorrento, which is full of orange groves, orange trees covered with fruit, and with lemon groves, and we wandered along the shore for four miles—a most delightful walk, looking down on to the blue waters of the Bay of Naples —until we got to a little place called Massa, looking across to the island of Capri. Here there is a grotto where there is a little entrance to a cave, and to enter it we had to lie down at the bottom of a little boat, a fisher- man's boat, and it was not a very clean one. There were scales of fish lying at the bottom, and we had to lie down flat on our backs to prevent our heads being knocked off as we went into the cave. (Laughter.) We went on to Ainall, where is the Hotel Cappucini, cut out of the solid limestone rock. We slept in one of the cells formerly occupied by the monks—it was once a monastery —and a very comfortable bedroom it was. The monks in those days knew how to make themselves comfortable, and they always selected beautiful places. Out of this hotel you walked along a terrace 200 yards long, with trellis work over it to shelter you from the sun. We wanted it, too ; in the month of November we were glad to have shelter. I was sitting there at ten o'clock in the morning, writing home, and the sun was so hot that I had to get an umbrella to keep the heat off. While we were at Amalfi we met Giovanni Barbaro, and he acted as our guide, and pursuaded us to go and see the Temple of Paestum. There we saw the oldest ruin that we had viewed the whole time. It is a temple 2,500 years old and the columns are some forty to fifty feet high, and some are seven feet in diameter. The building is as perfect to-day as is the Public Hall in Warrington, although it is 2,500 years old. We took our lunch inside this old temple, and very much we enjoyed it. I just thought I would let you children hear a little of the country we had been visiting, and of the beautiful climate_ But, after all, there Is some-; thing wanting there that you have got here. We saw no Sunday Schools, and we saw nothing done for the children. As a rule they are left to run about, and Italy, beautiful country as it is, has a vast lot yet to do in the way of education for the people. That is a great drawback there. While you find more beautiful scenery, and more interesting buildings abroad, yet, after all, there is no country, take it all round, equal to old England. (Applause.) Giovanni acted as our guide, and asked us to take him with us as far as Rome. When ' we got to Rome he begged to go to Florence, and then he begged us to take him to England, because every' Italian thinks that if he comes to England ha will make his fortune, and the great ambition there is to learp the English language. We could not refuse his persuasive manner, and we said we would bring him and see whether he would succeed or not. Before the night is over I shall ask him, with your permission, to sing you the Amalfi boat song. (Applause.) I am sure you will be delighted with it. (Loud applause.) Mr. MONKS, in the course of a short address, mentioned the recent death of on of the Sunday school boys, named Beddard. He had been requested to perform the burial service, and wrote to the Rev. S. Wilkinson say- ing that if it would cause any displeasure to his church he would gladly ask him (Mr. Wilkinson), or some other friend, to discharge the duty. In reply Mr. Wilkinson wrote:—" I always think that the feelings of the rela- tives of the dead should be consulted, so please by all means bury your old scholar on Thursday.' (Applause.) Mr. HILL then presented Mr. Crosfield with a copy of the Bible. On behalf of the donors he said that on that memorable occasion they felt that they might well pay Some tribute of the great esteem in which they held Mr. and Mrs. Crosfield. The teachers and scholars believed that Mr. Crosfield would accept the gift, not • because of its money value, but because of the feelings of respect that prompted them to make it. (Applause.) Mr. WooLutY, in making the second presentation, said that they all felt very much indebted to Mr. Crosfield for the benefits he had conferred upon that school. He wished to present the hymn book to Mr. Crosfield as a token of the esteem and respect of the teachers and scholars. (Applause.) . _ -

Mr. CnosrueLD, in reply, said :—I am exceedingly obliged to the teachers for their kindness in presenting to me and Mrs. Crosfield this Bible, and this hymn book. I do not think that they could have given us anything that we should have appreciated so much, because, as a speaker said, the Bible has a value beyond the value of any other book. (Applause.) It is not because of its money value, but it is because of the feeling which this present indicates—a feeling which 1 know is in your hearts—sf thankfulness that you have been allowed to teach the young in this Sunday School. I must say that the speaker has said more of me than he should have done, because my portion of this work has been merely the building of the school, and I con- sider the services of the teachers as beinr, infinitely greater to the children than anything that (have ever done. I thank you also on behalf of Mrs. Crosfield, and I am sure that she will value that book as long as she lives. (Applause). Itis bound to produce a feeling of affection between her and the teachers, especially the female teachers of this school. (Applause,) You know that from the first I always laid it down that this school should be open to anyone, of any denomination. I would not consent to have the school kept merely for one sect, and the consequence has been that we have in the school, children of almost every sect that there is in the town. It is that universality of religion that finds such an echo in my heart, because I take the bible as my guide. (Applause.) I say that you may search the bible through, and you will find that the teaching of religion was, to all people over all the face of the earth, irrespective of creeds and of sects, and the less we have of creeds and sects, the more there is of sympathy between Church- men and Dissenters, the better it willbe forthe people. (Applause.) I was delighted to hear that short letter from the Rev. Mr. Wilkinson. It does him credit, and it is exactly the lettet that I should have expected him to write, bemuse I know Mr. Wilkinson of old, and I know that he Itas a tender and good feeling towards the Services that are being performed in this school. (Applause.) Again I thank you most heartily for the kind presents you have made this evening. (Applause.) During the evening a short programme was gone through. It included a pianoforte duet by Master G. and Miss E. Crosfield, and several songs and recitations. The choir was under the conductorship of Mr. Frank Williams. The Amalfi boat song given by Giovanni Barbaro was much appreciated, and he gave a second song in answer to a recall.

QUITE A SECONDARY CONSIDERA:roxf..--Major Bouncer: "Alt, my dear younv lady, did I ever tell you about my adventure in Africa? No? Well, I was up a palm tree one day, and when I had reached nearly the top, lost my hold, and fell. If my friend, Captain Spiriting, hadn't been below to break my fall, I shouldn't be here now for the Christmas festivities. However, here I am, safe and sound. Ha, ha!" Gertrude: "Yes, but what became of Captain Spifkins?" Major Bouncer : "Oh, Spifkins He was buried out there, of course. Couldn't bring him home, you know." POOR UNFORTUNATE EIGHTY-EIGHT Dark was the destiny, rough the fate Of poor unfortunate Eighty. Eight. O'Brien's breeches and Sexton's prate Distracted the brain of poor Eighty-Eight. Biggar and Gladstone and Doctor Tanner, , Behaving alike in a shameful manner, Addled and worried the bursting pate Of poor unfortunate Eighty-Eight. Filling the cup of the twelve months' sorrow To the brim, bedad ! and what's more, bagorra Pity, oh. pity the woeful state Of poor unfortunate Eighty-Eight A Christmas session of wild debate Completed the anguish of Eighty-Eight. Let him begone, with no more annoy, Pelt him with pudding, the dear old boy— Martyred he was by Milesian rogues, And done to death by their greasy brogues. 1, (lfoonsAine.) THOSE CHRISTMAS BILLS.

Those Christmas bills those Christmas bills, how they do empty all our tills of 7 money saved for rainy time, and leave us each without a dime. Those pieces bright must pass away, and many a heart that erst was gay, while they reposed within the cells of safe and s'ecretaire, ex- pels a sigh or two, a swear, a groan, for those sweet cents, and dollars flown; while every hour the postman fills afresh the letter-box with bills. And then the plaguy Christmas-box, us out of time completely knocks; then come the Income Tax and rates, and oh, alas! the Christmas waits; and so this sort of thing goes on until we to the dogs are gone. He is stated to be an accomplished musician and a clever man, who has turned his atten- tion to living without work..

In Stepney two men have drawn up an agreement to the effect that "they hereby decide, for the satisfac- tion of both parties, to exchange wivetz, the said wives being perfectly agreeable to the carrying out of such arrangement." It is stated that the compact had its origin in one of the women becoming enamoured of the other woman's husband. The parties are now living together, apparently well satisfied with the novel con- ditions.

div.head: SATURDAY. DECEMBER 29. 1883.
div.p: SATURDAY. DECEMBER 29. 1883.

The Christmas of 1888 has come and gone, and there has been average merry-making if not aver- age weather. If there happens to be a green -yule, there is always a good deal said about the absence now-a-days of old-fashioned winters, old- fashioned in this case meaning a winter of hard frost and deep snow. There are some old-fashioned
People who stoutly contend that there is quite a
'change in the climate since they were young; but the meterological records do not. give support to ifly Such supposition. It is possible—it is even trobable—that our climate is undergoing a
tgradual change, but the change is so slow as not

to come within the ken of even the oldest inhabi- tant. The centenarian has a long span relatively to most of his fellows, but it is short, indeed, com- pared with such a cycle as covers a climatic change. We are not about to say that the Weather this Christmas comes well within the average; for that is not se. It is indeed Phenomenal; plants are putting forth buds; some of them are in flower, and even fruit trees are Ilcossoming. The present writer on the day before tlaristmas Day walked into, a friend's garden, in forth-east Lancashire, and gathered a little nose- yof primroses and pansies which were growing, the phrase is, "in the open." It may not.be Tory exceptional to find a primrose in flower, but 'it is surely rare to find the lovely delicate pansy in. bloom at Christmas. It is a green winter; but a green winter—so the adage has it—makes fat churchyard. What is meant by this, we suppose, is that when the frost and snow do tome they will find people, especially old people, unprepared, and therefore the more likely to be eut oft suddenly. Cold too is unfavourable to the development as well as to the diffusion of disease egerms; it is bracing to those who are strong, and therefore health-giving. But there is another side to the green winter, as the poorest of the poor Well know. It means that there is loss need of food and of fuel, and that scanty clothing can be made to do duty for a little longer without taxing the scanty exchequer. The poor, it is grailfying to know, are getting to _ _ .

.., more and more considered at Christmas-tide. There is more money to spend upon them because there is more to spend on charity, as upon every- thing else. A nation that adds one hundred - each year to its wealth should have some- thing to spare for the unfortunate, and even the nuprovident,who cannot see their way to a square Ineal on Christmas Day. Hence the Dinners to Poor People at this season, of which happily We now bar something every year. In addition , to what is done officially—such as the dinner given --ill the Mayor of Warrington, on Tuesday—private lvolence is everywhere more or less in opera- There are special subscriptions, in many

/48438,. in connection with places of worship; and, as hinds of this kind are usually distributed With discrimination, there is an increased chance s•the deserving poor, being made happy on what toight otherwise be a miserable day. Amongst Ahose who can afford it, there is, it cannot be .'denied, too much in the way of eating and drink- .ing at Christmastide. They pay the penalty sooner latter for the trespass, and, as the penalty is fitable, those who are tempted to over-indulge :_WOuld do well to 'reflect that a wider distribution 14 what they regard as good cheer would be good :1W round. It would certainly be a relief to the Poor, and they might find it would be a relief to ,111aMaelves. There are peOple who will be sceptical Wi to doctrine of this kind; but before pronounc- -1.4 against it, let them put it in practice. There yet time; Christmas is past: but we are on 'the threshold of the festival Of the New Year.

Lord DERBY'S speech at the Liberal Unionist AeMonstration at Liverpool, last week, has at least had the merit of exciting a considerable amount •IX controversy. It has stimulated the activity of 5 objectors to MT. GLADSTONE'S Home Rule le upon one important point—that is as to 'What is to be done in London with the Irish mem- 'bilre when they get a Parliament on College Greene they to be confined to Dublin, or are they also t° he permitted to take part in the debates at West- kinster ? There was a good deal said in the -ly days of the Home Rule agitation about the Justice of excluding the Irish members from the .3-1211Peria1 Parliament. We were told that the olsh would never stand it, although their leaders Ware anxious that the experiment should be tried. Liberal Unionists were more Irish than the Irish themselves; they were determined to save

from the tyranny of taxation without repre- Peatation; and so persistentlywQs thepointpressed that there were some who affirmed that their Phjections to the Home Rule Bill would cease, if :* GLADSTONE would yield on the question of the 111 Presentation of Ireland in the Imperial Parlia- .4lent. Mr. GLADSTONE has yielded; he recognises ;that there are difficulties whatever course is ,tahen; but he has made it clear that he • will :laot stand in the way of proposals to enable Fla Irish members to take part in the Imperial °tallness transacted at Westminster. And now a 'll.,ew class of objectors has arisen—thosewho, like •I•donn DERBY, believe that it will be impossible to ,devise any scheme that will work satisfactorily and .Pliable the Irish members to have a voice in 14nPerial affairs. He contends, with no little force, that any Government would be in an unfortunate

position if, whilst retaining the confidence of the representatives of Great Britain, there was a con- stant risk of defeat through the accession of the Irish members when mstters of Imperial magni- tude were under consid9ration. LORD SALISBURY some time ago, in his grimly sarcastic way, called this process a turning on of the Irish tap, and suggested that it would not be good for anybody. But his lordship is scarcely a typical citizen; his detestation of Irishmen, and of "black" men, is too pronounced. Still, the difficulty is one which will require facing, and we frankly confess that we see but one way out of it. If Ireland is to have a
Parliament Of her own, and at the same time have

a finger in the Westminster pie, she will be privi- leged to a degree which will not be satisfactory, in the long run, to either England, Scotland or Wales. Then, what, it may be asked, is the remedy? and we answer that the remedy is to give Home Rule to Ireland and extend the principle to England, Scotland, and Wales. LORD DERBY sees that this is a way out; but he is a timid politician, and he does not like it. He says You have proposals for Home Rule for Scotland; you may be quite sure that Wales will claim an equal concession to what it calls its nationality. If anybody believes that in these two little islands there is room for four separate natibual Govern- ments with one Imperial Government over them all—five Cabinets and five Parliaments —and that all those Cabinets and Parliaments can continue to work amicably together, he must be of an excep- tionally sanguine disposition, or possess the happy faculty which some politicians have of being able to shut his eyes very hard. We say not only that there is room for "four separate national Governments and one Imperial Government" but that no other plan has been proposed which meets all the difficulties of the case. What is wanted is not the faculty of shut- ting the eyes very hard, but of opening them very wide. "Elevate your vision," and you will find that a prospect otherwise harsh becomes harmoni- ous and pleasing. It is no use being frightened with names. What is a Parliament but a repre- sentative body for doing legislative work If it is a subordinate Parliament, it receives powers which are either delegated to it, or imposed upon it. It is not disputed that legislative powers can be given to Ireland as they have been given to Canada and a score of other dependencies, and if they can be given to these places they can be given to England, Scotland, and Wales. As well might it be argued that we ought not to set up County Councils, because there are already a large number of School Boards, Boards of Guardians, and Town Councils, and that it is impossible they could all "work amicably together,' It' is a question, in part, of national. sentiment, and, mainly, of the sub-division of labour Under both heads, a good deal may be urged in favour of the proposal. As Lord DERBY admits, already there is a demand for Home Thile on the part of Scotland ; and that, we take it, is because the Scotch feel not only that their business is neglected, but that when it is done it is not done so well as they could do it themselves. Lord SALISBURY was almost pathetic the other day, in his reference to the way in which Scottish business has been neglected; and there was ample promise of amendment. But what hope is there, in the ordinary course of things, of the pledge being redeemed? Little or none. And so with Wales ; she is organising to make herdemands felt, because she is not getting measures which she has for years been pleading for. Lord SALISBURY , had quite a long story to tell of the measures which the Government were prepared to pass, when the opportunity was given them. His , list was certainly suggestive, but it was more suggestive that he finished it with the remark that he should have to go on for ever if he were to speak of all the measures that were ready and could not be passed. The PRIME MINISTER, be it remembered, spoke of minor reforms which are outside the Liberal programme, and, when the Liberal programme is added, the pile of arrears is absolutely appalling. LORD SALISBURY'S remedy is reform of procedure—more closure; but Parliament is already sufficiently closured. There is a limit to the application of the gag, and that limit has been reached. The fact is Parliament can not overtake its work; it is blocked—blocked beyond the., possibility of permanent relief, except by Home Rule all round. We move now-a-days so quickly, and our complex civilisation raises so many new issues, that no Liberal can say there would not be plenty of work for four Home Rule Parliaments and an Imperial Parliament. The Tories can't see this; they never do see things; it is the way with them to do nothing more than they can help doing. It is for the Liberals to see and to act—to show themselves, in a word equal to the many problems that are pressing for a solution.

The young Duke of Newcastle is going to marry —not " Yum-Yum," but Miss Candy. It is his first love and his last; he showed an etzly liking for candy.
The House of Commons rose on Monday; there will be the schoolboy's holiday of four or five weeks; and then "at it again." The worst of it is so little gets done, and there is so much to do.

The "World" says :—" The Duke and Duchess of Westminster have a large family party staying with them at Eaton Hall, where they have arrived from visiting Lord and Lady Leicester at Holk- ham. They intend to remain in Cheshire for nearly two months."

At th 9 Annual Sessions for Lancashire, on Thursday, the question of allowing Dr. Rogers, chief medical officer of Rainhill Asylum, a pension of £BOO a year, was considered; but no decision was arrived at; the matter was adjourned. So that snake is scotched—if not killed.

Mr. Walter Besant has been caught ;tripping. i He has been making the moon rise n th'e east at two in the niorning. But a novelist must have something novel, even if he has to rise (with his moon) at two a.m. The difficulty is that there are readers who will have fact even in their fiction.

The Marquis of Ripon has been contrasting the progiammes of the Conservative and Liberal parties, as set forth respectively by Lord Salisbury and by Mr. Gladstone and Mr. J. Morley. Con- trast is easy but necessary. ' It is sufficient to name the features of two programmes to contrast them. One to the other is as thin water gruel" is to "roast beef an. plum pudding."

The Twenty-Fifth of December is known to all Christians as the clay of the celebration of the birth of Christ; but not all of them know that them is nothing that can be recognised as evidence that "the Saviour of the World" was born on the 25th of the month. It is a point upon which there has been a good deal of controversy, some arguing for one day—some for another; and the outcome is— " All that we know is—we do nothing know."

The misletoe and the yule log are part and parcel of Christmas association as if they were in some way or other bound up with the event, and, yet, strictly speaking, they are an excrescence. They belong not to Christianity, but to Druidism; they are survivals of what some would call Paganism. But the Pagans showed themselves wise in burning a yule log to keep themselves warm; and as to the rites, or rights, of the mistle- toe we cannot do without them; they may be Pagan, but they are very pretty.

Mr. and Mrs. John Crosfield had an enthusiastic reception at the Bank Quay Mission Room. on Wednesday evening. After the presentation of a Bible and Hymn Book, Mr. Crosfield gave an account of his tour in Italy. His speech will be found in another portion of the paper. His des- criptions are graphic and vigorous; he goes straight to the point ; he has something interest- ing to tell, and it will be seen that he tells it in an interesting way.

The natives of India have been discussing their grievances in a National Assembly, at which over one thousand delegates were present. The Presi- dent, in his inaugural address, claimed that the concession asked for was moderate—namely, that half the members of the Legislative Councils should be elected, and the remainder nominated by the Government, one-fourth being officials. This is not too much to ask for, and ought to be conce- ded. We should show ourselves wise, and wise in time.

According to a London Correspondent :—" A confectioner in a northern suburb has on sale 'Sunday toys '—bricks for building churches, chapels, and Sunday schools, but which could not be used fot any more secular purpose." There is a story told of a smart little boy who, when he was reproached for playing with his "bricks on a Sunday, said he couldn't be doing wrong—he was building a church with them. Can it be that the wide-awake boy has- grown into a wide-awake tradesman.

Thrilling details are given in our columns, to-day of the wreck in the Bay of Biscay of a Newcastle steamer, the Storm Queen; and of the burning of a Missisippi steam-boat. In both cases, there was sad loss of life; and in both cases the captains perished through remaining to the last at the post of duty. It is some eonsolation in these calamities to know that noble men have nobly done their duty in trying to save the lives of their comrades. Whatever may be said of the Age of Chivalry, the Ago of Heroism is not yet passed.

The Emperor of China is to be married on February 23rd. The Dowager Empress wills it so, and when the Dowager Empress says a thing is to be done, it is as good as done, you know. She had her way in giving the throne to her nephew, and now her nephew is betrothed to one of her nieces. Like the great Earl of, Warwick, the Dowager Empress has shown herself to be a king maker; and now she lets it be known that marriages are made in China as well as in heaven. What a mother-in-law she would make I

There is so 'little hope of any good coming of our slaughter of Arabs at Suakim that it would be well before going much further if John Bull would put his "studying cap" on. Mr. John Morley has a definite opinion' on the subject. In a letter to the Secretary of the International Arbitration and Peace Association he says: "We are going to spend English and Egyptian money, and to sacrifice English, Egyptian, and Arab life, without the pretext of a single definite advantage to any English, Egyptian, or.krab interest."

There will be a total eclipse of the sun on New Year's Day. What is the use of having a New Year's Day if it does not eclipse its predecessors P There was a like phenomenon on New Year's Day 1612 (new style) and we are promised the third on New Year's Day 2,161. Rather long to wait, but there is no harm in naming the matter. Perhaps it is as well to mention; too, that sun-gazers need not get their smoked glass ready on Tuesday; the eclipse will not be visible at Greenwich, or "i' England," as" Ab o'th' Yate " would say.

• It is agreeable to find that the rumour as to the suspension of half-a-dozen Warrington constables is nothing more than a rumour, and we need hardly say that we regret having given wings to the fable. Mr. Chief Constable Taunt writes:— 01 can assure you no constable has been sus- pended in this force for drunkenness, or anything connected with a public-house, since the 17th May last, when the man was dismissed from the force.' The Chief Constable knows, and we, of course, accept his statement. We gave the rumour for what it was worth, and it seems it was worth nothing.

Mr. Wilfrid Blunt has just issued a volume of poems, some of which were written whilst under- going imprisonment for fighting the battle of freedom in Ireland. The following sonnet strikes us as striking a true and tender note : To do some little good before I die; To wake some echoes to a loftier theme: To spend my life's last store of industry On thoughts less vain than Youth's discordant dream; To endow the world's grief with some counter-scheme Of logical hope which through all time should lighten The burden of men's sorrow and redeem Their faces' paleness from the tears that whiten. To take my place in the world's brotherhood As one prepared to suffer all its fate; To do and be undone for sake of good, And conquer rage by giving love for hate; That were a noble dream, and so to cease, Scorned by the proud but with the poor at peace.

' CHESHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL: DARESBURY DIVISION. —A third condidate for the honour , of representing the Daresbury Divisibn on the Cheshire County Council has entered the field in the person of Mr. W. R. tarp, of the Tannery, Preston Brook. He does so in answer to a numerously signed requisition, and, in his address, points out that he is a ratepayer , and employer of labour in the division, and has a knowledge of the requirements of the district. If elected, he adds, he would work earnestly for the joint and common welfare of all classes.of the community. He does not ask support from any political party, and will be uninfluenced by political considerations. To workingmen he promises the same sympathy, consideration, and assistance, as to the wealthiest amongst them. PENKETH WESLEYAN SCHOOL. Last even- ing week, an entertainment was given by the scholars of the above school under the able manage- ment of Mr. J:Watson, the head master, assisted by the assistant mistress, Mrs. Wilson, and the pupil teachers. The programme consisted of songs, pianoforte and violin solos, musical drills &c., and the cantata entitled" The Glad New Year." Each of the four seasons was beautifully represented by as many young ladies with flowers and fruit emblema- tic of their parts. Each Season, also, had the three months belonging to the respective seasz•ns who each in a solo expressed their allegiance to the New Year. Afterwards, the scholars who had success- fully passed their examination by lI.M. Inspector were presented with a beautifully illuminated certificate by Mr. R. Garnett, J.P., one of the managers. Mr. Garnett spoke of the great pleasure it gave him to present so many certificates, 'and expressed his opinion that for its size there was not a more successful school in Lancashire. Mr. D. Garnett was then called upon to present to the pupil teachers the prizes they had gained by pass- ing their Government examination successfully. Of these Miss M. S. Routledge (fourth year and Miss M. Mainley (second year) had gained "Excellent," each receiving .£3 as grant from Government, and Miss E. M. Ashton (third year) "Good," receiving.£2 grant. Of this grant a third was expended by Mr. Watson in the purchase of books which were, on Friday evening, presented to the teachers, together with the certificates of drawing which they had gained, Miss M. S. Routledge having passed in perspective, Miss E. M. Ashtcua and Miss M. Seed in freehand, and Miss M. Mainley in both perspective and freehand. Mr. D. Garnett expressed the pleasure he felt at giving to the teachers thcir prizes which all knew were fully deserved. Mr. R. Cook proposed a vote of thanks to the performers, and expressed his satisfaction with the entertainment. The enjoyable evening then closed with the singing of the l`Tational Anthem,

- - At Widnes Petty Sesgens,..onTriursday, before Mr. H. Wade Deacon, Michael Simeney, a labourer, was again brought up on a.charge of having feloni- ously, wilfully, and With- malice aforethought, attempted to kill and murder: his daughter Ellen Sweeney. Catherine Lancasterissingle woman of 13 Peel-st, said the prisoner- and' his wife and family came to live at :.her house on the Bth December. On Tuesday the 18th December the prisoner arrived home about half-past ten at night. Mrs. Sweeney, and her daughter Ellen were in the parlottr -at the time. When Mrs. Sweeney heard • her husband at the door, she ran into the kitchen. The prisoner, who was very drunk came into the parleaw, and he asked the child, who was sitting on . the side of the bed that was laid on the floor, where her motherwas. She replied " Stre has just gone out—not.many minutes." " Here you young devil" said the prisoner will take your. life, I will make you tell where she lai"' and at the same, time he struck the girl on thetead with his fist, the blow.', knocking her prostrate on the bed:. He then kicked her on the body with the side of his deg, and lying upon her he seized her throat in -Ilia hands and preased jt until her tongue protruded. The girl: screamed as welt as she could and witness pleaded. to iitisoner to desist but he would not. She .than heard Mrs. Sweeney- ask another inmate of the house named Roach to go and "save Ellen before he kills tore' ' and: Roach entering the room dragged the prisoner off 'his. daughter. The girt- = t•-em the house in terror,. and fell fainting in the middle of the road. There- were. the marks of the prisoner's hands on her throat and her lips were di.. coloured and much swelter). She-was afterwards taken to the surgery of Dr. Hutehinson, who attended to her injeries.—Ellen Sweeney, .aged' eleven years, also gave evidenee. She showed a diSpesitien to screen her father, but her statements confirmed the testimony of 'the previous witness. She-said she had seen her fatherill. .use her mother on . several' occasions. She usually lived with her grandfather at Wigan, and had' only been with her -father- and mother this title- since the fifteenth Deoembcr: Shevolunteered the state- ment that when her father • assaulted her,she was very' ill and weak in consequence of a, kick she had received' on the previous Saturdaynight,when a man kicked' her' by mistake.—Thomas• ROachi described how he released' the girl from the clutches of her-hither, and Dr.-Hutchin. son, testified to the seriousiniuries she had received,- he prisoner was coannitted'totake his trial at tiwnest Quarter Sessions.

The whereof the tradesmen's estahliahments were closed. In the early part of the day the weather-was bright and mild,butin the afternoon and evening there was a heavy:. rainfall'. In consequence of- this open and " unseasonable' weather the pinch orpoverty has not-been so severely felt in the town as usual, and none of those charitable schemes for- providing breakfasts. and dinners for the poorer children have been so far been put in operation; but considerable private benevolence has been.- displayed. In the morning divine service was. held at the churches and several of the chapebe In the afternoon a Miscellaneous concert, promoted by the Simms Cross Primitive Methodist Cgapek was given in the Alexandra Theatre. In the evening under the same auspices, the "Messiah" was rendered by the Cam- brian Vocal Union.

RUNCORN THEATRE Royet..7--The • character of the entertainment-at the Theatre Royal during the past week has been in keepiiig- with the • festivieseason, and good audiences have assembled each piglet to•wttness the per- formance of "King Christmas and the Good Fairy." Mr. Butler Stanhope, the lessee,, had spared no pains to place the piece upon the stage iu creditable style, and the various scenes represented were the "'Snow clad house of King Christmas," Enchanted glade by Killarney's ' Lakes, "The haunted' Wood." &o. The play was of a very entertaining- and amusing description, and the rollicking fun and quiet humour of Patsy Connor, the comical cobbler (Mr. Stanhope) was especially appreciated ;,his bettor half, Betsy Connor, was well pourtmyed, by Mrs. Stanhope. The requisite sentiment was introduced by Fergus Ger ald (Mr. Henry C. Ward) and the-Fair Monica. (Miss Sarah Millwood). whilst Mr. Leslie Douglas was a capital success as thia wicked Michael Stoneheart, Esq. The other characters: were also in able. hands. Mr. Stanhope had pressedi into his servide quite a host of children, who acted as, Leprecsoms, fairies, imps, and Lilliputian soldiers, and their quaint costumes and comical antics were a source of much merriment, whilst their singing of chorusea dm., was: an ec,nal source of pleasure. The piece will. be repeated this (Saturday) evening. The successful drama" Drink ' is announced for next week. ANNUAT.,CLEARANCE SAAF, IS now being and, W. Dutton, Sankey-st , Warrlngton.—Adrt. ST. JOHN'S PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH, Ru-nolui.—On Christmas Day, at *t. John's Presbyterian Chapel, Ruu corn, a tea meeting was held in connection, with the Band of Hope. About 130 persons sat down to, tea. The tabs were presided over by Mrs. Outhwaite, Miss Hayes, Miss Clough, Mrs. Dobson, Miss Hermon, and Mrs. Evans. A fter tea an entertainment was given, the emir being taken by Mr. Houghton. The choir opened the meeting by singing "What a meeting of the loved ones," which was heartily ,applauded, after which Mr. James Richardson gave a song, in which the members of the choir joined in the chorus. There then followed a recitation by Mr. R. Harrop, entitled " The Old Maid (in character), which caused much amusement. Mrs. R. Evans gave a song in her usual good style, and this was followed by a pianoforte solo by Mr. G. Bowyer, entitled" Sabbath Evening Chimes," which was encored. The Chairman (Mr. Houghton) then gave the song "My Polly," and, on being recalled, sang " I fear no foe. Mrs. Timperley gave "The Maid of Langollen," after which the glee party sang "The Sleighing Song,' followed by a quartette by the Outhwaite family and Mr. Bowen, entitled " Profundo Basso," which received an encore. A quartette by Messrs. Richardson, Warbur- ton, Dobson, and Outhwaite was then given, after which the choir closed the meeting by singing" The future lies before me." Subsequently games of various descriptions were indulged in, and a most pleasant and enjoyable evening was spent. The greatest eh-ristism festival of the year--: ifitristmas—was ushemdin the old Cheshiro town. ha accordance with, ancient custom. From the steeple of the Parish . Church the bells rang forth a joyous peal, and a, concord of sweet sounds was borne on the midnight air from the throats of numerous parties.. of MO singers. The weather was not" seasonable.' knstead of a cold crisp air- and glistening. snow, the atmosphere was very mild, and the ros,ds were black and muddy; and its the day wore on rain descended in tearente and continued far. many hours. Except for those operations.which must of necessity be carried, on in the chemical works, business was entirely sus- pended, and the townspeople were evidently spend- ing thew,Christmas at their own fireside, or at the houses.of friends and relatives as Ore. streets wore a most, deserted aspect. In the morning divine service was conducted at the Parish Church, and in the evening, a choral service was rendered. There were fairly good congregations. Services were, also conducted at the Catholic Chapel and at saveral of the Noncon- . flormist places of worship. Christmas cards were as much if not more in vogue thanever, and tha work of the officials was • enormously increased. The postmen commenced their rounds at a very early hour; but it was net until half-past two in the afternoon that the last missive was delivered at its destination. The Council of the Warrington, Ccerservative Association held an adjourhed- meeting, in the Assembly Room of the Conservative Clun„ on Satur— day evening. The question before the members was the desirability, or otherwise, of contesting the three divisions into which Wearington is.divided in the matter of representatiodnn the Lancashire ,County Council. At the previous •areeting ot the Coun- cil the names of Mr. John White, J. 11,, and Mr, John Fairclbugh, J.P., were before it as 'possible candidates, Mr. Fairclough being the suggestrit.• nominee of. the Town Council. Mr. Fairclough • then intimated, that he was in a difficulty so far as theyartv wancon- ,cerned, owing to his being a noakinee- of the Town 6, Council, but rather than appear in opposition to another Conservative he would withdraw hi S - name: After k considerable discussion it was resolved that Mr. J. White should be adopted as the Conservative -candidate-for the southern division which comprises the south-west, south-east, and Latchford wards. It iraaibelieved that a contest would be avoided by Councillor •F. A. Roberts, (Liberal), and Councillor Monks (Liberal Unionist) being nominated for the two northern divisions.

div.head: LIBERAL MEETING. –
div.p: LIBERAL MEETING. -

A meeting of the executive of the • Warrington. Liberal Association was held at the Liberal Club, ois • Wednesday evening, when there was a good atten— dance of members. Councillor A.- Roberts. occupied the chair (in the absence of Mr. McMinniee who•was prevented from attending by:indisposi— ,tion) and explained the situation with regard to the- 'County Council elections. There was,- he said, no, 'provision in their rules for dealing with such a matter' as county council representation, as that 5V58 entirelx a. .new thing, and it had been thought undesirable to bring - The members together until they saw. what course ;events were likely to take. Mr. McMinnies and several other gentlemen acting in their private capacities, had' suggested three names, namely, those of Mr- John 'White, Mr. F. Monks, and his own. So far as the Con- .servatives were concerned, he understood:that they had , resolved to adopt Mr. White as candidate •for the, , southern division, leaving the two northern divisions to- '_thire their own course. The Liberal putty, as a party,, wasnot committed to anything that hath.hitherto been done; and it was open to the members to consider the ' whole question on its merits. A good deal of discussion, then, took place •as to whether it was desirable or- rat to-have a contest at the present juncture. It was. tecegnieed that the three gentlemen named would make toierably fair representation of the tewn, but those present did not feel they were in a position to pass any resolution on the subject, although there was ..a strong feeling that Mr. F. A. Roberts, at any rate) should be nentinated-for the north-west .division. It was. ultimately resolved that the party should take no action at the present time, beyond deciding that the executive saw no reason to take exception to the three gentlemen who had becn.norned to represent the e Ivision. WIDNES A. v. WIDNEIS--4;7-hiaar's.--Playekl on the ground of the former. Widnes kicked off from the entrance end, and the St. Mary's charging down gradually, worked the ball down to the Widnes goal, securing a minor soon after and then a try, from which no goal resulted. St. Mary's here scored a goal from a free kick. Score at half time—St. Mary's 1 goal, 1 try, 2 minors; Widnes, 1 minors. Final score: St. Mary's 1 goal, 1 try, 2 minors; Widnes, one goal 1 minor. Winaas V. Hur.t.—Theso teams met at Hull. The first half was very evenly contested. Teal scored, but Kilburn failed to improve the point. After the interval, Hill ran in, Jackets's place-kick being a failure. Subse- quently play was carried on in the home territory, and they-were forged to say. Hill dropped a splendid goal, and the game closed in a victory for Hull by 1 goal, 2 tries, aad 2 minors to .1 minor. Widnes were short of Plumpton and Hewitt. H. ASHTON'S TEAM v. Sr. PauVs.—These two teams, both of which were were of a miscellaneous character, met on the Wilderspool ground on Wednesday morning, and played an even game which ended in a draw. In the first half St. Paul's did all the scoring, putting on a try and four minors. In the second half, however, the tables were reversed as Ashton's team scored two tries from one of which a goal was placed. Not to be outdone, St. Paul's played strongly towards the finish and secured another try which was converted into the major point. The game ended as follows :—St. Paul's, 1-1-4; Ashton's team, 1-1-2. WIDNES V. NEATIL—The second match in the Welsh tour of the Widnes club was played at Neath on Tuesday afternoon, in wretched weather. Kiddies was again unable to play for Widnes. Play was very fast. Widnes pressed at first, and scored two minors, having hard lines on several occasions. Then Plurnpton, of Widnes, had two ribs broken and retired from the game. Neath gained two minors and Emery nearly dropped a goal, the score at half-time being two minors each. In the second half Widnes had all the play and crossed the home line time after time. Smith and Clarke got trios, but they were not improved, being in bad positions. The home men were outplayed at all points. Final score: Widnes, two tries, and six minors; Neath, three minors.

WIDNES v. LLANELLY.—ThiS match took place on Saturday, at Llanelly, in wretched weather. Widnes were short of Plumpton and Kiddie, and after a twelve hours' journey were in poor form. Llanelly were minus Roberts and Dan Griffiths. Early in the game Llanelly przssed and secured two minors, and then Morgan obtained a beautiful try and placed a goal. After fur- ther pressure Llanelly registered a mine', and the score at half time stood; Llanelly, 1 goal, 3 minors ; Widnes, nil. In the second half Widnes attacked the home line repeatedly, and Clark ought to have scored. A minor followed to the home team, after which Pitt scored, and Morgan failed at the place. The play, notwithstanding the apparent advantage to Llanelly, was even in the second half. Result :—Llanelly, 1 goal, 1 try, 6 minors; Widnes, nil. Reeceitie v. nIIRTOI4-ON-TRENT.—This match which had beenloaed forward to by the Runcorn people,vras played on Wednesday. Evershed started, and the play cen- tred in the Burton quarter. A run and pass by Woods, and the ball went in touch near the line. On the throw out, Hancock crossed the line, but Brazendale failed at the place-kick. Minors now fell freely to the home side. Lowe, Evershed, and Deakin put in good work for Burton. The homeforwards shone prominently, Faulkner, Broady, and Gayter being well to the front, but the interval came without the score being increased. During the second half Runcorn pressed, and near the close of the game Wainwright scored a try, but Woods failed at goal. The game, which had been pleasantly fought, terminated in favour of Runcorn by 2 tries and 8 minorS to 1 minor. RUNCORN "A " TEAM 17. STOCKPORT "A" TEAM.-^ Played at Runcorn, on Saturday, before a moderate attendance of spectators. The Stockport team arriving early, Runcorn commenced with only twelve men, the remaining three putting in an appearance during the first half. The game was very one-sided throughout, and ended as follows :—Runcorn, 3 goals, 4 tries. and 6 minors; Stockport, 1 minor. Teams :—Runcorn, S. Booth, full back; E. Lunt, J. H. Crompton, and H. Cawley three-quarter backs ; S. Abrams and .1. Honing- worth, half backs ; J. Gatley (captain), Dutton, Barker, E. Andrews, Lee,T. Abrams, R. Hailwood,T. Whinyates, and Tipper, forwards. Stockport : Bownell, full back ; Mills, Standring, and R. Downs, three-quarter backs ; Clegg (captain) and Plant, half backs; Bardsloy, Heyes, Hamilton, Morley, Downs, Daniels, Beswick, and Bennet, forwards.

SrocicrOnr V. RUNCORN.—PIayed at Stockport, on Saturday, before about 3,000 spectators. Potts, for the home team, set the ball in motion, and a good return followed up br Runcorn took operations into the Stock- port quarter, but the home team retaliated, and thereby took hostilities inside the visitors' 25. Runcorn quickly worked the ball back to centre field, and from thence inside the Stockport quarter flag. Ogden and Ankers on separate occasions relieved the pressure, but the visitors were not to be denied, and they ultimately rushed the ball over the line, a dead ball accruing to them. This was quickly followed by another minor to Runcorn. On kicking out again, marks were made by H. and W. Hughes and Faulkner, the latter of which Brazendale kicked dead. The home team were still obliged to play a defensive game, which they did with very great tact. A smart piece of dribbling by Parrott took proceedings out of their quarter into the visitors half. Long kicks were now indulged in, the ball eventually landing in tho home half, and a scrimmage ensuing the ball was worked further towards the Stockport line. Some combination play, however, on the part of the homesters relieved their citadel and took operations to centre field; again the visitors began to press, which ended in them scoring another minor. Up to half the game was mostly in favour of Runcorn, who added two minors to their credit, the score now reading Runcorn six minors, Stockport nil. Resuming from centre, the visitors tried their utmost to score a major point, but the defense of the home team was splendid, for they continually repelled all their opponents advances'. The ball in turn visited each half, but Runcorn held the advantage by again visiting the Stockport redoubt ; a good dribble by Scho- field relieved to centre. Davies neutralized by getting possession of the ball and rushing on to the home line, whew he was tackled by A. Bruckshaw, the danger being averted for a time. After a short stay in the home half Wainwright made tracks for the enemy's line, but Ozden stopped his career. A. B:uckshaw was new prominent with some running and kicking ; this was responded to by a complete rush with the ball over the defenders' line, Taylor saving further disaster by kicking dead. The drop out was a slight relief to Stockport'. Rit,son, following the ball up the visitors' half, put in his kick, which was nullified by Brazendale, who was in grand form' running the ball out of their 25 and kicking to centre. Runcorn following up their advantage took hostilities close to the home line, where Stubbs attempted to drop a goal, the ball going dead. The visitors still continued to play a forward game, Parrott and Ogden being of great service in relieving the home line. Another minor fell to Runcorn by a combined rush of the visitors over their opponents' line. A splendidly contested game resulted in [a ,draw in Runcorn's fay our by nine minors to nil. . _ _

WARRINGTON v. Baouoirrois (A Tuams).—Flayed at Broughton. Two thirties being agreed upon, and Broughton winning the toss, Warburton kicked off for the visitors, his kick being charged down. The home team at once commenced to invade the visitors' territory by rushing the oval in touch near the corner flag. Daniels obtained possession, and put in a short kick. Immediately afterwards Bibby made his mark and caused play to rage in neutral territory. Speakman got hold and made a nice run and put in a good kick. Monnock was next conspicuous by a splendid run, which caused play to rest in the visitors' half. From a scrimmage Mather got away and passed to Warbur- ton, who made a nice run, but was brought down by Whitely. A series of scrimmages took place, which ultimately found the visitors pressing the home team close to the line, from where Beard succeeded in gaining a try, which War- burton converted into a goal. Resuming from half- way, the kick off was returned to centre. The visitors kept gaining ground by successive scrimmages, from one of which a nice bit of pr.ssing was witnessed between the 'Warrington backs. A free kick for Broughton carried play to centre. Ashurst, Sumner, Beard and Eyes headed a grand dribble up the field. Shepherd saving nicely. From the pack Williams secured and passed to Mather, who transferred to Daniels, the last-named being collared by Dalton. The Broughton forwards broke away, Jolley averting danger by punting into touch. Ashurst was next conspicuous by a splendid dribble up the field, which carried play to the home 25. From the succeeding scrimmage Williams passed nicely to Mather, who transferred to Speakman, and good following up on the part of Bibby enabled the last-named player to score a good try, which Warburton again improved by kick- ing a goal. Through some off-side play the kick off availed nothing. Soon afterwards Daniels got posses- sion, and made a nice dodgy run and kick, to which Whiteley responded by kicking into touch. This brought about half time the score being Warrington two goals to nil. Restarting, Smith kicked off for Broughton, Jolley getting in a good return kick to Whiteley, who punted into touch. From a scrimmage Warburton dribbled the oval up the field, and kicking over the line scored a try, but through seine misunder- standing the referee gave in a minor. Daniels replied to the drop out, play resting in neutral ground. Mannock got away with a nice run, but was checked by Bibby. Soon afterwards a rush by Ashurst, assisted by Warbur- ton and Bate, forced Whiteley to concede a minor. For a short time the game was operated in the Broughton half, where a series of scrimmages were carried mostly by Warrington. Broughton were allowed a free kick for some infringement. Williams caught nicely, making his mark, and Warburton made a good attempt from the place kick. Whiteley kicked to Daniels, who took a drop at goal, a minor ensuing. Shortly after the drop out the visitors were again invading the home territory. Subse- quently Warrington forced their opponents to resort to

the saving clause. Hassell was next conspicuous by a grand run, but was timely checked by Daniels. From a scrimmage Sumner got possession of the oval, and made a short run up the field, Dalton tackling him. Shortly : afterwards Williams made a good attempt to drop a goal, a minor resulting. On time being called the score stocd las follows :—Warrington two goals and five minors; Broughton, nil.—Teams :—Warrington: T. Jolley, full back; Bibby, Speakman, and Daniels, three-quarter backs; Mather and Williams, half backs; Ashurst, Creaghan, Warburton, Hayes, Ryes, Sumner, Molyneaux, Beard, and Bate, forwards. Broughton : Whiteley, full back; Hassell, Smith (captain), and Dalton, three- quarters ; Mannock and Shepherd, half backs; Sepsford, Sadler, Dickson, Clarke, Goldsmith, Norton, Smith, Jones, and Campbell, forwards. WARRLNGTON VERSUS MOSSLEY. These two teams met at Warrington on Bank Holiday (Wednesday), in the presence of a great crowd of Spectators. Warrington were weakened by the absence of Dillon (captain) and Littlowood from the forward ranks, but nevertheless they played strongly, and, indeed, the game was one of the closest and most exciting that has been seen on the Wilderspool ground during the season. From the kick off play became very fast, Warri a- ton soon beginning to press severely and the visitors had to concede two minors in rapid succession. To this result some creditable play on the part of Antrobus largely contributed. Some clever dribbling by the visitors then gave Evans an opening which he improved upon by some well-judged kicking. A free kick next fell to the lot of Warrington near their opponent's quarter- flag but an assay at goal-dropping by Fair Turner was charged down. The visitors again invaded the home territory, but Povey was instrumen al in relieving. Lawton securing from a pass by Billings, made a splendid run over half the field but he was finally grassed by Evans and Jolley, and the Warrington lines were again relieved. Fast give and take play followed, a long kick and ready following up by Ashworth threatening the home lines, but Evans relieved by cool and well-judged play. A fine pass from a scrimmage by Antrobus gave Barnes a chance of making ground, the latter again passing to Massey who ran over but the ball was ruled back. Half-time was called witk the score—Warrington 2 minors ; Moseley nil. The second half opened favour- ably for Mossley, but a smart tackle of Lawton by Barnes helped the home team to again relieve their lines. After a good deal of even play Lawton made a fine drop at goal the ball just going a little wide. The rest of the game mainly consisted of hotly contested scrimmages, but Ila.rnes showed up in some fine kicking and dribbling causing the visitors to kick dead. The final result was —Warrington 3 iniaors, Mossley one minor. Teams : Warrington : full back, Evans ; three-quarters, Jolley, Barnes, aad Massey; half-backs, Speak:nan and Antrobus ; forwards, 11. Ashton, Fair Turner, W. Povey, Ashurst, Nevins, Frank Turner, C. Unsworth, Handles, and Teare. Mosssley : full back, Kneen ; three-quarters, Ashworth, Lawton, and Flowers ; half backs, Billin<Ye and Neild ; forwards, Winterbottom Mayall, W. Newby,' H. Newby, Walker, Makin, Rowan, and Cox.

div.head: WARRINGTON v. BROUGHTON.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. BROUGHTON.

This match, which is always welcomed by footbal enthusiasts in tho Warrington district, took place on Saturday, when an enthusiastic crowd of spectators assembled at the Wilderspool enclosure. As both sides were strong a grand game was expected, and in this respect the spectators were not disappointed, for the play from start to finish was of a most interesting nature.

Payne started operations by kicking off to Jolley, who replied with a run and kick to the halfway flag. The visitors now made away from the line-out, but Massey replied by a grand run and kick to the Broughton 25. This splendid piece of *ork by Massey, coming so soon after his accident against Moseley, called forth loud cheers. Sofiano relieved, only to find a barrier in Speak- man, and a forward movement, in which Ashton and Dillon were conspicuous, placed the " vrirepullers " in an aggressive attitude. Slowly but surely the homesters took the leather to the Broughton line, when a good kick by iticDoUgall was replied to by Jolley. A free kick to the visitors afforded relief, but a drop at goal by Evans almost had the desired effect, and to save further disaster Totnlinson touched down. Broughton from the drop out went away with great dash, and. a neat dribble by Wormald ended in a mihor being credited to the visitors. A faint reply was made to Frank Turner's drop out, and Speakman displayed excellent judgement by a neat kick into touch at the Broughton quarter flag. Pretty passing by Antrobus, Speakman and Barnes gave the latter a chance, but his shot at goal went wide of the mark. Fair Turner made a grand reply to the drop out, and Barnes effected a pretty run to the Broughton line, slipping when just on the point of scoring. The ill-luck that attended the efforts of the Warringtonians up to this point of the game was very discouraging,both to the team and their supporters, but they struggled manfully, and a well-executed dribble by Ashton and Littlewood again menaced the Broughton goal. Barnes foiled Payne, and after a neat pass to Massey, the latter had an ineffectual shot at goal. Exchange kicks were next witnessed by the opposing backs, but Evans settled the play well in the Broughton quarters by a grand kick. Maasey had another abortive shot at goal, and soon after a similar shot by Barnes struck the bar, rebounded into play, and Massey, securing possession, got over near the corner flag, the kick at goal failing. Barnes was again to the fore with a smart run, and after Payne had raised the hapes of the Broughton contingent, the home forwards by a combined rush swept down on the Broughton fortress, Dillon having hard lines in not securing a taegible point. However, from the follow- ' ing pack Speakman passed accurately to Antrobus, and the latter feigning to pass easily dodged the Broughton back, and secured a well merited try, Barnes failing at goal, the latter point bringing about half time, the score reading Warrington two tries, four minors, to Broughton one minor. Frank Turner re-started the second half, and no return being made the Warringtonians, by smart following up, took the oval over the line, and the Warrington skipper (W. Dillon) in the first minute grounded at the corner flag, Massey making a poor attempt at goal. Again the Warringtonians pressed the visitors but Wormald by a spirited run took the oval to neutral territory. Passing by the home backs neutralized the effort, and Unsworth came in for notice with a smart tackle, which prevented Prince from clearing his lines. Smart dribbling by ' Ashton and Dillon forced Broughton to save. Soon after a combined rush to the visiting lines ended in illnsworth scoring, but as in the previous instances, the kick at goal failed. The Broughton team ROW played up with renewed vigour, and from the restart Wormald and Rome took the ball to the Warrington end, where a minor resulted. Two more minors quickly followed, the (outcome of long kicks by Tomlinson. Not to be denied, the visitors still attacked the Warrrington goal, and relief was only brought about by a smart run on the part of Barnes, who dashed away, being finally grassed at the half way flag by Prince. Continual rushes of the Broughton forwards caused Warrington to defend, and a pretty run by Wormald was finally rewarded by Lodge securing a try in the last minute of the game, but failure attended the kick at goal. This item brought about 'No-side," the final score reading—Warrington, 0-4-5; Broughton, 0-14. Both teams are to be complimented on their display, and, as in previous matches, every department in the Rugby game was shown to advantage. On the War- rington side, all the backs played well. Evans was particularly safe at back, whilst all the three-quarters passed and kicked with excellent judgment. The half backs were exceptionally tricky, and their well executed passes called forth great praise. In the forward divi- sion all worked with untiring energy, and foremost amongst others were Dillon, the brothers Turner, and Ashton. On the Broughton side, Wormald, Sofiano, and Rome were the most prominent. _ _

Teams: Broughton: R. 'Tomlinson, back; J. H. Payne, F. T. Prince and P. M'Dougall, three-quarter backs •C. Rome and Summers, halfbacks; A. Sofiano, P. Lodge, J. Jackson, R. A. Green, F. G. Wormald, W. Glendinrung, F. G. Dixon; J. Buckley, and E. H. Smith, forwards. Warrington: J. W. Evans, backs; J. Jolley, T. Barnes, and J. T. Massey, three-quarter backs; W. Speakman and A. Antrobus, half backs; H. Ashton, Fair. Turner, Frank Turner, W. Povey, R. Littlewood, W. Nevins, C. Unsworth, W. Bandies, and W. Dillon, forwards. Referee, Mr. S. Bagshaw, Swinton F.C.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

It will be agreeable news to lovers of football in Warrington that the fixture of the local team with the Maoris has been changed from Wednesday, the 16th of January, to Thursday the 17th. Wednesday being market day in Warrington was about the worst day in the week for this important engagement, and the local committee are to be congratulated on having succeeded in getting the date altered. There is sure now to be a record gate to witness this match. Rochdale Albion first team can now claim the honour of breaking the hitherto unbroken record of the War- , rington "A " team. The two teams met at Rochdale on ' Wednesday, and the result of a tough encounter was a victory for the Albion by one try and two minors to one minor. The Albion can, however, not claim to have won entirely on their own merits, as nearly half the r team was composed of specially selected players from other clubs. On the other hand the Warrington con- tingent was greatly weakened by the absence of several of its best hands, one substitute being picked up at the railway station just before the team left. In addition to I this the home team seem to have had the referee on their side, as two tries were disallowed the visitors who were also debarred from the benefit of two free kicks in very favourable positions. la spite of all the disadvantages they suffered under, the Warringtonians played with a good deal of their old dash, but the combination, in which they are particularly strong, was spoiled by the muddy and slippery state of the ground. The match on the Wilderspool ground this afternoon, between Warrington and Leeds Parish Church, ought to be a particularly good one. The visitors are in the front rank of Yorkshire clubs, and it will be interesting to s=e if the local team are any luckier with them than with wakefield Trinity, the last lot of Torkshiremen they encountered.

div.head: ST. JA.COBS OIL FOR VETERINARY PURPOSES.
div.p: ST. JA.COBS OIL FOR VETERINARY PURPOSES.

Owing to the great popularity attained by the use of St. Jacobs Oil in other countries for veterin- aay purposes, the proprietors, The Charles A. Vogeler Company, of 45, Farringdon-road, London, have determined to introduce this famous remedy in Great Britain for that purpose. They distinguish the Oil for veterinary purposes from that for human use by placing the former in a yellow wrapper, while the latter is put up in a white wrapper. The public are particularly cautioned to use the Oil in YELLOW WRAPPERS ONLY for veterinary purposes, as same contains ingredients particularly adapted for use on horses, cattle, and dogs, and Is far supe- rior to all other liniments and embrocations for veter- inary purposes. The price of the Oil is within the reach of all, viz., two shillings and sixpence per bottle, of all dealers in veterinary medicines, or free by parcels post from the proprietors. We should most certainly say, from the enormous popularity which the Oil has attained, not only in this country but in every part of the civilized world, that no stable or kennel will be complete without St. Jacobs Oil in yellow wrappers. The West-End Omnibus Company, of Auckland, New Zealand, of which Mr. S. Child is manager, writes to ' the Daily Herald of that city:—" We have much pleasure in bearing testimony to the efficacy of St. Jacobs Oil for veterinary purposes. Its success has been particularly marked in the cases of lameness in our stables. For man and beast, St. Jacobs Oil is WI greatest pain-curer ever discovered." The Trotting Editor, the Spirit of the Times, New York, after an exhaustive interview with leading horse- man, stablemen, sportsmen, drivers, and breeders of horses, states, editorially, that St. Jacobs Oil will do all that is claimed for it in the cure of sprains, stiffness, lameness, and suffering in man and boast. The popular veterinary surgeon of New York, Dr. William A. Sonia, D.V.S., for nine years in charge of the Third Avenue Tramcar stables, certifies to the curative ' qualities of St. Jacobs Oil, as*-superior to all other remedies for all ailments of horses, ...ouch as sprains, galls, and rheumatism.

div.head: BUR-NING OF A MISSISSIPPI STEAMBOAT. HEARTRENDING SCENE.
div.p: THE BUR-NING OF A MISSISSIPPI STEAMBOAT. HEARTRENDING SCENE.

NEW Yonx, WEDNESDAy.—Tht first reports of the burning of the Mississippi steamer prove to have been somewhat exaggerated. It is now thought that the loss of life will not exceed twenty. The accounts of the disaster are full of horrible details. The steamer was near Plaquemine, about one hundred miles above New Orleans, when the fire was discovered. It was then about midnight, and most of the passengers were asleep. The fire was discovered by a negro boatman, who gave the alarm. The steamer was laden with cotton, which was in a very dry condition, and the flames spread with fearful rapidity. They sprang from bale to bale like flashes of lightning and shot up through the cabin and over the sides, enveloping the entire boat. The alarm had been sounded at the first sight of fire, the whistle being blown and the bens rung, but within three minutes from its discovery the vessel was one sheet of flame from stem to stern. The scene that ensued was terrible in the extreme. Men yelled and ran about the deck like maniacs; others, screaming at the top of their voices, threw themselves into the river. The chief clerk, Mr. Powell, went to every door, and made certain that the passengers and hands were awake, and urged them to hurry to the front of the boat before they were cut off. They did so, but were thrown into confusion by the darkness of the night, the blinding smoke, and their own fright. The smoke was so thick and suffocating from the high piles of burn- ing cotton that a number of persona, in trying to force their way to the bow, were overcome by it, and fell suffocated on the deck, where they probably died before the flames reached them or the boat sank. In the mean- time the crew were fighting the flames as best they could, but without suee6g. The steam pumps were worked, but had litttle effect on the fire. The flames soon reached the engine-room, bursting the steam pipes and releasing great volumes of steam that severely scalded several of the men who were driven from the room. The engineer and his assistants clung to the sides of the boat. The pilot had headed the steamer for shore as soon as the alarm sounded. As she liadla full head of steam on at the time she was into the bank in two or three minutes. Then the pilot jumped out over the bales of cotton, and springing into the river, swam ashore. The captain, crew, and passengers had fought their way to the front of the boat, getting scorched faces and bruised limbs. The majority of them sprang from the boat when she was about ten yards from the shore,and the moment she touched the rest leaped into the mud or water. The steamer rested for a moment aground and then swung around, drifting down stream and burning uutil she finally sank. Although the crew had escaped from the burning boat they were not all saved. Both the captain and Bob Smith, the famous pilot of another burned steamer, met their deaths after getting ashore. They sprang into the mud on the bank, and becoming fast were slowly roasted to death by the intense ;heat from the burning boat. They buried their faces and hands into the soft mud to protect themselves, and appealed to the people on shore to come to their assistance. This, however, was impossible. The captain was !finally protected from the fire by means of a box, and was dragged ashore with ropes. It was too late however ;2 he had suffered too serious injuries, and although he received medical care at once he died before he reached Plaquemine. Bob Smith had figured in several steamboat accidents, and to his courage in sticking to his post on his own burning steamer to the last moment was due the saving of many lives on that vessel.

After the chief clerk had aroused every person on the vessel he returned to the bow, but his escape there was cut off. As a last resort he sprang into the water, and although he could not swim, managed in some way to get on to a floating bale of cotton, but two deck hands jumped on to the bale also and turned it over. Powell fell into the water and was drowned. His body was found in the river twenty miles below Plaquemine this morning. John Crofton, the carpenter, was in the upper portion of the boat struggling to get near the bow. The flames were twisting and sweeping all about him, and soon enveloped him. He fell and was burned to death before the eyes of the people, who were not able to render him any help. Others met with their death while forcing their way to the bow of the boat, being overcome by the smoke, or were burned to death while fast in the mud, or drowned. The boat was about fifteen yards from the shore when the intense heat compelled almost all the crew to spring from her. Seme reached the shore, and tried to climb the steep, muddy, and slippery levee, but were caught by the flames before they could do so. Others clung to bales of cotton in the river, but in many instances the bales floated against the burning vessel, and the occu- pants were either roasted to death or compelled to let go, drop into the water, and drown. It is believed that the fire was due to a careless smoker, who threw a cigarette among the cotton. The steamer is valued at 18,000 dollars, and the cargo at 12,000 dollars. Both are a total loss

(3) COLLISION IN THE MEMEL—The Red Cross liner Maranhense, leaving the Mersey on Wednesday for the Brazilian ports, ran into the Isle of Man mail steamer Snaefell, which was at anchor nearly opposite the landing stage. The Snaefell's plates were crushed below the water line, and the boat, which had its forward compartment filled with water, was towed to the Albert Pier and beached.
