On Thursday morning two ironworkers were frightfully burnt at the Maryport Hematite Iron and Steel Works, Cumberland, by a quantity of molten metal ejected from one ot the furnaces. A water pipe had burst, the water flowing into the furnace and causing a loud explosion. Several men had narrow escapes. At Barnsley, on Wednesday, John Ogden, butcher, was fined £5 and costs.for haying in his possession a quantity of beef unfit for human food, and yet in course of pre- paration for sausages. SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT A FAIR. On Wednesday night a boy named Michael Dempsey, aged 12, was watching a performance outside a boxing booth at Car- diff fair, when a rush was made. The boy was knocked down, and falling on a peg with which the booth was fastened to the ground, it penetrated his skull, and he died on Thursday morning. ATTEMPT AT MURDER AND SUICIDE AT LANCASTER.—A young woman named Isabella Ramplin, daughter of a Lancaster artist, is in custody on a charge of attempted murder and suicide. On Thursday afternoon she left her parents' house, taking her infant, six months old, with her. Bome lads were on the canal bank near Lancaster when they saw the young woman throw the child into the water and then jump in herself. Three boatmen were sheltering from the ram some distance off, and were attracted by cries for help. One of them, Thomas Cummings, plunged into tke canal and brought the child to the side. A rope was thrown over the head of the mother, and she was dragged to land. She I remained unconscious nearly half an hour.

div.head: LOSS OF LIFE.
div.p: LOSS OF LIFE.

On Wednesday evening the survivors of the screw steamer Storm Queen, belonging to Newcastle, were lauded at Dover from the Norwegian barque Gul- nare. The Storm Queen was lost in the Bay of Biscay on the 22nd instant, with the captain and five of the crew. The survivors when rescued were in a very exhausted and destitute condition. ' Twice they had a narrow escape from death. The j survivors number 22. The vessel was on her way j from Sebastopol to Rotterdam with a cargo of grain. Soon after entering the Bay of Biscay, on the 21st, the ship experienced a fearful storm, the sea beimg , described as running mountains high. The vessel became unmanageable, and ultimately the captain gave orders to man the boats. One was smashed before leaving the vessel, and the remaining two could only be got away with the greatest difficulty. The captain, Mr. Jaques, long refused to leave the ship, although the boats stood by her several hours. Five of the crew, who could not be induced to leave the vessel, remained with him, and the captain and the rest perished after having tried to save them- selves by moans of a raft. An attempt was made by the survivors to reach the raft, but before they reached it the whole of the men were washed off. After being washed about by the sea until the morn- , ing of the 22nd. the Storm Queen was geen to sink. The survivors on being landed at Dover were taken to the National Sailors Home, where they were well cared for. After their immediate necessities had been attended to they were forwarded by the chaplain, Mr. Pearce, and the superintendent, Mr. Davison, by free passes granted by the South- Eastern Railway Company, to their destinations, mostly in the North of England. Francis Eliot, chief officer, who was suffering from injuries sustained in the disaster, states that the vessel was bound from Sebastopol to Rotterdam with a cargo of rye. Her tonnage was 1,374 tons register, and she carried 28 hands all told. The vessel was built at Wall- send in 1880, and belonged to Newcastle. Proceeding, the officer stated :—All went well until we reached the Bay of Biscay. We had previously experienced very severe weather. On the evening of the 21st December we ran into a very terrific north-westerly gale. The sea was tremendously high, rolling like so many mountains. I have passed through the Ray many times in a storm, but never experienced anything like it. The heavy waves swept the ship from stem to stern constantly. One tre- mendous sea struck her with such violence that her cargo was shifted and put the vessel on her beam ends. We at once made every possible effort to shift the cargo' back by breaking through the holds and the cabin bulkheads, so as to be able to get below. It was not till then that we found that there was a tremendous I rush of water running into the vessel. The ship I gradually listed further over, and the in rush of water j increased. I could then see the peril we were in. But still we did not give up trying to save her. I set the sailors to work to try and pump out, but the vessel filled too rapidly. I tried to get from one hold into another, and was almost drowirNl in doing so. The water was just under my chin, and it was with great difficulty that I kept myself up by holding on to the side of the vessel. Finding that it was utterly useless to attempt to do anything further, I ran to the boats. Our captain ordered all hands to assist me, and told everyone to try and save themselves, but exhorted us to be as cool and steady as possible. We launched one boat safely with nine hands in it. We had three boats on board, but the violent sea had smashed one to pieces like so much matchwood. We could not get the other launched for some time, and when we did get it out it had to be shoved off without the crew. We were now in terrible danger of losing our only hope ef saving ourselves. The only thing left was to jump into the sea and swim to the empty boat, which many of us did. It was a most thrilling spectacle to see the men jump off one after another into the fearful seas, not knowing whether they were going to a watery grave or whether Providence would aid them to reach the boat. There was not the excitement one might have experi- enced, but it was quite enough for me, and I shall never forget it. I was in the water forty minutes before the boats were able tø find me. Our captain, Mr. Jaques was a brave young officer. He would not leave the ship. He said he would not leave her until he saw that everyone was safely off. There were five others on the Storm Queen who were afraid to leap from the ship into the sea. The captain was standing on the bridge when welast saw him. Our two boats remained by the steamer from 10.30 p.m. on the 21st until between 1 and 2 a.m. on the 22nd. We then found that the boats would not much longer stand the tremendous seas. We shouted to the captain and the remainder of the crew to make another attempt, but they would not do so. There were 13 men in the other boat, but there were only nine in ours' and there would have been plenty of room for them. Some time after, before daylight, we sighted a ship. It proved to be the Nor- wegian barque Gulnare. We shouted and tried to pull towards her. The seas prevented us for some time, but we were ultimately taken on board. Upon reaching the barque the boats struck against her and went to pieces. We were hauled on board by means of ropes. I got a very heavy blow on my leg which is still very bad, but I didn't think much about it then. It was life or death for all of us. The barque stayed near to the Storm Queen during the whole of the night, in the hope of rescuing the remainder of the crew. We saw the cap- tain and men on tke steamer next morning, but the barque could not get to her—the storm was too violent. It was too dangerous to lower a boat. It was about 10 a.m., I should' think, on the morning of the 22nd that we attempted to lower a boat for the remainder of the crew. The wind was blowing with hurricane force and prevented all efforts About an hour after that the steamer foundered and we sighted the crew on a raft. The captain of the barque used every endeavour to steer aloneside the raft. We drifted about for some time. The raft was often lost sight of amongst the waves for five or ten minutes together ; then we would see it rise to the top of the waves. It was heartrending to see the poor fellows so close, and yet we were unable to reach them. At one moment we saw the raft rise with a tremendous swell. Then it disappeared, and when we saw it the next time the whole of the men had disappeared. The barque then sailed about for a con- siderable time so as to do everything possible to save the poor fellows. Everyone was satisfied that no more could be done, and we proceeded on our. voyage. I must speak in the highest possible manner of the great kind- ness we received at the hands of Captain Eilerssen and his crew. They gave us clothing and food. All many of us had on were our trousers and shirts. . .

_ The second engineer, who is the only survivor in that department, stated that the water rushed into the engine- room with great force and put out the fires. It was about eight o'clock when the water in the ship rapidly increased and became overpowering. He climbed up the rigging with several others, so as to jump into the water clear of the ship. He heard the captain shout "Keep a good heart, my lads, and you'll be saved ; keep steady." He jumped into the water, and was pulled into the boat by an oar.
Before leaving Dover the chief mates and the rest of the survivors indicted a letter to the captain and crew of the barque, expressing their gratitude for the humanity displayed by them. •*-

DESPERATE ASSAULT ON POLICEMEN. At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Monday Thomas Monition, hawker, Turner-et., War- rington, was put in the dock to answer charges of having been drunk and disorderly in Turner-st., on Sunday evening, and of having assaulted Police- sergeant Bowen, constables Westhead, Millington, I and Taylor, and two civilians, named Thomas Critchley and Edward Noon. Prisoner, who seemed to treat the matter as a joke, pleaded guilty to all the charges. The case for the prosecution was stated by Sergeant Bowen, who said that on Sunday evening he was on duty at Town's-end, when a woman came and complained that her husband—the prisoner—was making a regular football of her. He had gone into a neighbour's house, and witness went in after him. Prisoner threatened the officer and took up the poker, btft it was wrenched from his grasp. He afterwards came out of the house, and witness put him into the entry which led to his own house. Prisoner thereupon invited the officer in, and threatened to murder him. The officer was turn- ing away when the prisoner rushed after him and struck him a violent blow with a piece of iron. Wit- ness parried the blow with hisistaff, but apiece of flesh was taken out of his hand. The two then closed, and fell on the ground, where the fight continued until the other presons assaulted came up to render assistance. On the way to the bridewell prisoner knocked right and left, and as he was being put in a cell he assaulted Constable Taylor. The Sergeant, at the conclusion of his evi- dence added that he was very sore from the treatment he had received.—prisoner: It's a pity you aiT not worse ; what about what you have done to me.—The Sergeant: If I had not had the presence of mind to ward the blow off it might have killed me.—Prisoner It should have killed you, and then you would have been done with.—The Mayor, in passing sentence said : As a warning to others who may be disposed to enjoy themselves in the same way at Christmas we will give you the heaviest punishment in our power. You will be committed to prison for six months with hard labour.— Prisoner: Thank you, sir. Why don't you give me another six for it?

_ At the same Court, a youth, named John Mannion, a hawker, of Warder-st., St. Helens, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly in WinwiCk-st. on Saturday night; and having assaulted P.C. Corbett. Defendant was creating a disturbance, and on being taken into custody he struggled violently with the officer. The two wrestled together on the ground, and in the struggle the defendant bit the officer's thumb to the bone.—The Bench characterized the assault as a very savage one, and sentenced him to one month's Imprisonment with hard labour.—John Thos. Mulcrow, Buckley-st. vow also charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Winwick-st. on Saturday evening; and with assaulting P.C. Buckley.. Defendant was in company with Mannion, and when the ifficer appre- hended Mannion, he attempted a rescue, and gave P.C. Buckley several violent kicks.—He also was sent to gaol for one month, with hard labour.

Writing to the secretary of the Birmingham Liberal Unionist Association, Mr. J. A. Bright says there is now a possibil- ity that his father may live for some time, and even that he may gat downstairs again. Sir,—llnfortunately for me the assailant in the attack on a Warrington musician gave in his name as Frank Williams, and as certain unscrupulous persons, who though they know me to be innocent in the matter, have endeavoured to use the above to my hurt, will you per- mit me to inform the public, through your columns, that the matter is in no possible way connected with myself, and that I am not the Frank. WiWain* Yrll9lie c9waretiy assaulted my old frie.id Herr Prreger. The inisertion greatly oblige,—Yours, Ago., FRANCIS WILLIAMS. 3, rowN,i-st., Warrlngton, 28, 12, 1888.

THE WARRINGTON PARISH CHURCH. Sir,—Of late there have been various rumours afloat in the town to the effect that the new Rector has begun to introduce objectionable ritual in o the services at the Parish Church. I sincerely hope that that is not the case, because there is no doubt that Ritualism and Catholicism are not far removed. It may be possible to steer a middle course by introducing a mild style of ritual, but I think the Rgtor will do well to consider the matter before he inflicts on the parishioners cere- monial that they do not care to have, and which, as he may find, they will not have. The Rector has power to do pretty much as he likes in these matters, I suppose, but it would be very unfortunate if he happened to lose his congregation.—Yours, &c., PROTEST. December 27, 1838.
THE IMPROVEMENT OF ROADS.

Sir,—Will you allow me through your widely-circula- ting columns to call the attention of those of your readers who are ratepayers, to the opportunity afforded by the forthcoming election of county councillors, for impressing upon the candidates who seek to represent them, sound views upon the very important question of the maintenance and repair of our main roads, which, after the Ist April next, will be under the control of the county councils, and also for exacting pledges from them that they will, if elected, support the adoption of some more efficient and uniform system of repair than that at present adopted by the majority of our road surveyors. It has been amply proved, and is generally admitted by competent authorities, that our roads could and ought to be maintained in a much more efficient con- dition than they are at present, at a very much less cost, if the work were done in a more skilful and systematic manner. Pamphlets fully explaining the system advocated by the Roads Improvement Association, and leaflets for dis- tributiod amongst electors at forthcoming meetings will be supplied free on application.—Yours, JOHN E PHILLIPS Hon Sec
• Roads Improvement Association, 57, Basinghall-street, London, E.C.

THE NEWTON-IN-MAKERFIELD COUNTY ELECTION. Sir,—Early next month the county electors of the Earlestown and Newton district will be called upon to exercise the privelege they possess of selecting one whom they would like to represent them on the new County Council. As the matters to be dealt with by the Council • will be of great interest to county ratepayers may I ask them, through the channel of your paper, to carefully weigh the probable result of the contest before coming to a hasty decision as to whom they will vote for. To my ~. mind it seems that Mr. Pearson, of Golbome, is coming ." forward as a representative of the classes, while Mr. !I4t Rawlins, of Rainhill appears on the other side as the ":0.:4' candidate of, or for, the masses. Mr. Pearson's numina- tion emanated from the men of monetary influence at itlik.the meeting of the Newton Improvement Commissioners, while Mr. Rawlins' candidature was adopted at a meet- ing of workingmen. The latter were, admittedly, Liberals in their political opinions, but, apart from that consideration altogether, they were of the class which has a solid preponderance of votes in the electorate. This fact alone should lead anyone to suppose that they would • adopt some one who would look well after their own interests and those of their own class ; and there is no doubt Mr. Rawlins is the one gentleman who will do it. I therefore appeal to all working-men to support him on the day of election. He is thoroughly well acquainted with the wants and requirements of the district and his active connection in past electoral struggles eminently fits him for thr ')osition he now seeks to attain. His end and aim ii.^".dinirably set forth in the address he has issued and a perusal of this leads one to exclaim." He is the man we want " ! Then let us work td- secure his election—Yours, &c., A WORKING-MAN
Earlestown, Dec. 26, 1888.

NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS COUNTY COUNCIL CONTEST. Sir,—l think, seeing that a certain section of a political party- in this district have thought fit to oppose the nominee of the representatives of the people in Hay. dock and Newton, it is only fair that the moderate politician and non-political class should have something to say in reference to this contest. There can be no doubt that the nominee of the Newton' Improvement Commissioners, and the Haydock Local Board, is recommended by them on general grounds and not from political motives, as the offer was in the first instance, offered to other gentlemen previously, of both political opinions. The ratepayers having failed to obtain the sanction of their chosen representative to

stand (through reasons we all very much regret) I think it shows very bad taste indeed for a few of the Com- mittee of any political party to nominate, for party' reasons, a candidate in opposition. Their only reason appears, by their own showing, political party gain, theit opponent (although contesting without introducing in the smallest degree the political element) being a Conservative. Now I think we moderate politicians, are quite strong enough to decide the election, and I think it is our duty to upheld the nominee of the two Boards, who are elected by ourselves, and once and for all give such a blow to the political section referred to that wit' for ever deter it, or any other political section, from introducing politics in our local affairs. Surely we have enough in our Parliamentary contests without introducing them in our local matters, and a section, whose chief point is to vilify the character of a private gentleman is, I think, not worthy of support. Let us, therefore, throw in our support with such moderate gentlemen as Mr. Joseph Evans of HaydociK, Mr. George McCorquedale of Newton, and all the leading gentlemen of the district, independently of party.—l am, yours obediently.
NON-POLITICAL.
THE TORIES AND THE COUNTY COUNCIL ELECTIONS.

Sir,—However much the Conservative party may be behind the Liberals on questions of political progress, we as Liberals are,l think, compelled to yieli the palm to them in matters appertaining to party tactics. The Tories always adopt the plan of working on the public mind by undercurrents, and by attempting to mask their true political character until they are safely in position. An instance of this kind of party manceuvering presents itself by the way in which many of the candidates seeking election for the county councils are raising the "no politics "cry in order to secure the return of all the old set of Tory gentlemen—men, who think it a fair and right thing to sentence a poor wretch to undergo fourteen or twenty-one days' imprisonment for stealing a turnip, or three months for taking the life of one those Bratininical birds, the pheasant, or partridge. It is ra• her a curious coincidence, as Mr. McLaren said the other day at Sandbach, that whilst many of the influential Coaservatives, are pretending to ignore party considerations, and advising the ratepayers to vote only for ti k best and most experenced candidate, that candi- date should in the majority of cases turn out to be a high-and-dry Tory gentleman. But I am pleased to find that in a number of divisions, both in Lancashire and Cheshire, this dodge, has fallen rather flat. Our Conservative friends in this division of Fredsham, made a like move in bringing forward Mr. Reynolds and Mr. Baxter, on professedly neutral grounds, but Mr. Slater Lewis has, I think, well-nigh spoilt their little game in this division by adroitly coming out as a Gladstonlan Liberal. This has already had the desired result of bringing some of our Frodsham Conservatives and renegade Liberals out of , ambush, and I trust that we shall soon have the Tories with their candidate (Mr. Reynolds) on one side, and the Liberals, with Mr. Lewis, on the other—as for Mr. Baxter he may, I think, be compared unto a scout, whose only chances of success will ,depend on his ability in catching deserters from both sides. Unless the working men of Frodsham are blinder to their interests than what I take them to be, they will, when the polling day comes, plump for Mr. Lewis. The latter gentleman can lay claim to be doing something towards increasing the trade of Frodsham and the surrounding neighbourhood. But what has, or is, Mr. Reynolds doing in this respect 7—Yours, &e., PLEBEIAN.

LYNN. SUNDAY SCHOOL TEA.—On Wednesday the annual. treat was given to the children of the Sunday school. After- wards tea, games,songs, and recitations were indulged in to the delight of the little ones. CHRISTMAS AT LYMM.—A really seasonable Christmas :Day generally finds Lymm pretty well patronised by skaters and others, but Tuesday wats so damp and dreary as to discourage all outdoor methods of passing the holiday, and the village had a very deserted aranCO: Some perambulatory bands enlivened the neighbourhood, but otherwise the day passed over 'in a very quiet fashion. AssAcTITX6 A 151.iTCHER.—On Saturday, at the Lymth Pollee Court, before Mr. Stubs and Mr. Lister, ThomaS Birk pleaded guilty to striking John Hatton, butcher, on Saturday night, the Bth of December. Hatton went into a shop next door, where an altercation was taking place, and on interfering was struck by Birk. Prisoner said in defence that Hatton struck him first. He was fined 205., and 275. costs.. FUNERAL OF THE LATE Mn. ADDENBP.OOKE. —The funeral of the late Mr. Addenbrooke, solicitor, who died suddenly last week, took place on Monday afternoon, the remains being interred in the Parish Church burial ground. Prior to the burial a choral service was con- ducted ill the ehurCh. A large number of wreaths and floral tributes had. teed received, Mr. Addenbrooke having been much respected by a Lirgre circle of friends. ACCIDENT.—On Wednesday afternoon a young Irish- man in the employ of Mr. Edwin Massey, farmer,Clierry- Lice, Lymm, had his leg broken. A horse which was drawing a cart laden with manure reared and dropped on him, through being frightened by another horse with a milk cart belonging to Mr. James Marsh. The man was removed to the Warrington Infirmitry where on inouirY he was yesterday found to be progressing fa, -.bly

ParmirivE METHODIST TVA PARTY.—On Wednesday the members of the Lymm Primitive Methodist Chapel held their annual tea party. There was a good atten- dance at tea, the tables being presided over by Mrs. Evans, Mr. Thomason, Miss Rathbone, and Mrs. Ball. After tea Mr. John Thomason occupied the chair, and the scholars gave recitations, interspersed by music by the choir. The Rev. W. Evans gave an address en the value of Sunday school work. A SAD CASE.—At the Lymm Police Court,'.on Wednes- day, Elizabeth Sharpies, daughter of James Sharpies, was brought before Mr. Peter S übs, charged with wandering abroad. It appeared that the girl, who is 25 years old, was in service in Liverpool, but on Saturday night she was found by the police wandering about, and was taken to the police station, where her parents were communicated with. It was, however, found that her mind was deranged, and on Wednesday it was necessary to have her removed to the asylum. She was accordingly brought up, and on the certificate of Mr. Stubs and Dr. Williamson, was declared to be insane, and removed to Macclesfield asylum. STEALING A CHRISTMAS DINNER.—At Lvmm Police Court, on Monday, two men. named John Willanson and Alfred Percival. were charged with stealing a duck, of the value of 2s. 6d., the property of Mrs. Bates, of Thelwall, on Sunday afternoon. A witness named John Taylor stated that he was in company with the prisoners on Sunday afternoon. After they had left the Pickering Arms they went to Mrs. Bates' farm. They saw a duck in the yard, and Percival went and picked it up. He carried it about 20 yards, and than handed it to witness; who asked him if lie intended to steal the duck. To this he received no answer, but gave the wrd to Wilkinson, who carried it to New Field, Lymm, where he (Wilkinson) resided. Prisoners were each fined 10s. and costs 9s. Bd., or in default of payment, 14 eays' imprisonment. PRESENTATION TO THE REV. E. W. LOMAX.—The Rev. E. W. Lomax, who has resigned the curacy of the Parish Church, delivered a farewell address at St. Mary's, Lymm, on Sunday morning. On Thursday evening, at the Drill Hall, the rev, gentleman, who is greatly res- pected in Lymm, was presented with the following address, illuminated and framed :—" The undermen- tioned members of the congregation of the Parish Church of Lymm, and the mission-room, Statham, desire to convey to the Rev. E. W. Lomax, on his resignation of , the curacy of the Parish Church, after a period of six years' labour in their midst, the expression of their best wishes for his future happiness and prosperity. They beg 'his acceptance of the accompanying purse. and trust it will serve as a practical prcof of the good feeling which has always existed between them, as well as a small recognition on their part of the faithful and diligent manner in which he has discharged his duties, and more particularly towards the poorer classes con- , Med to his care." Then followed the names, with the amounts of 51 subscribers from Lymm, and 39 from Statham. The purse contained £7O contributed by the people of Lymm, and £lO 2s. by those of Statham. COMMENCEMENT AT ARPLEY. The devia ion of the Mersey from its present course to a straight line from the Iron Bridge, across Arpley Meadows, has at last been begun by the contractor. From thirty to fifty men are now employed near the Warrington Cricket Field in stripping oft the surface grass, cutting trenches, guiding lines, etc., and notwith- standing the start was only made a few days ago, and the Christmas holidays have intervened, fair progress has been made. The deviation commences near the corner of the Warrington Cricket Club Ground and runs in a straight line across Arpley Meadows ending just above Walton Arches. There Is a large amount of work involved and some considerable time will probably elapse before its completion. After the deviation, a portion of the disused river course will be occupied by extensive docks. It may be mentioned that on the south bank of the river deviation will run a new road, which, commencing near Wilderspool Crossing, will be a continuation of flit er-road, and after crossing the Ship Canal by means of e swing bridge, will run into the Chester-road near the Stag Inn, W lion. THELWALL, LYMM, &c. Very little work has teen done on these sections, the Christmas holidays caung a stop of several days. The men stopped work on Saturday, resuming again on Thursday morning.

EXPERIMENTS AT HOWLEY INTER-
CEPTING DEPOT.

As suggested by Aldermen Burgessat the last meet- ing of the Warrington Town Council, experiments have recently been made at the Howley intercepting depot, with a view to prevent the escape of effluvia. Yesterday afternoon week a number of mem- bers of the Town Council and other gentlemen met at the depiit, on the invitation of the Sanitary ' Committee, to witness the experiment. Among those present were the• Mayor (Alderman Sutton). Aldermen Burgess, Holmes, W ebster, Picirmere, Councillors Monks. Jenkins, Bolton, H. Roberts, Voisey, Wright, Garner, Heaton. J. Taylor, Dr. Gornall (medical officer), Messrs. Whittle (deputy town clerk), Longdin (borough surveyor), Walker (assistant surveyor), Hunt (chief constable), Norman (nuisance inspector), W. Diggle, S. Davies, Evans, and others. It will be understood that the closet pails of the town aro carried by vans to the inter- cepting depiits and the excremental matter they con- tain is emptied into receptacles whence it finds its way into automatic ejectors and is then forced by pneuma- tic pressure through pipes to the main depotatLongford, where it is turned into manufuactured manure. As every one knows, complaints have been made from time to time of the disagreeable smells emanating from the inter- cepting depots. These smells, it is understood, were caused very largely by the emptying of the pails, and the pre- sent experiments have been carried on with the view to remedying this. The process adopted, as explained by the Borough Surveyor, is simple but ingenious. Lines of pipes open into the receptacle into which the pails are emptied, and, by means of a fan which was worked by an engine, air is constantly drawn through these pipes and the suction thereby caused draws into the pipes the vitiated atmosphere and forces it out at the other end of the line of pipes. In its passage through the pipes it is carried through a cylinder containing disinfectants, and a the other end it is discharged into liquid disinfectants. Judging by the experiments just made, this has the effect of completely purifying the air from all mal-odorous effluvia, as when standing near the dis- charge end of the pipe not the slightest offensive smell could be detected. And, although vans were being rapidly emptied of their contents, the atmosphere of the depot remained remarkably pure and untainted. This was explained to be due to the constant influx of fresh air cansed by the working of the fan which drew into the pipes 2,300 cubic feet of aip per minute. As proof of this a joint in the pipe was broked, whereupon the atmosphere of the depot was very quickly impregnated with unpleasant odours. In answer to a question, Mr. Lencdin stated that the disinfectants in the cylinder would last twelve or eighteen months, and all that would be needed at the end of that time would be about a gallon of carbolic acid. Before the conipany dispersed, Alderman Webster remarked that the experiment had been very successful as far &sit had gone; and Coun- cillor Heaton said the Sanitary Committee had evidently solved one thing—they had succeeded in concentrating the smell, which was a very great deal to do. Coun- cillor Jenkins expressed the hope that the Sanitary Committee would be able to convince the residents in the neighbourhood of the depOts that they could live where they were in perfect health and comfort. Mr. Diggle also made some remarks, of a rather pessimistic nature, with regard to the experiment:

Fortunately she was not much burnt. PoliceeSergeant Walker and two constables entaeci the shop and put out the flames, the damage to the fixtures being slight. A number of the large business houses in the town of Marblehead, Massachusetts, were des•roy,ed by fire on Tuesday night. • Mr. Alexander Stephen has declined to come forward as the Unionist candidate for Govan, and it is now - believed that Sir John pender will contest the seat with Mr. Wilson. Stunmonses were on Wednesday served on Mr. E. Harrington, M.P., to appear at the Tralee Court on Monday. A branch of the Bristol and West of England Bank. at Torquay, was entered on Tuesday by burglars. They strove hard to get into the strong-room, but were dis- turbed, and escaped hurriedly, leaving on the premises several well-finished implements.

MR. STANLEY'S NATIONALITY. "One who Knows Better" writes to the "Times "One who Knows'! has been strangely misinformed as to the original name and early history of Mr. Henry M. Stanley. Ills birthplace was not Mold, but Denbigh, where he was born on Thursday, January, 28th, 1841. His mother, whom I well knew, was the daughter of a butcher in that town, and his father, John Rvwlands, was a farmer who lived at Segrwyd, in the near vicinity. The child was a great favourite with his maternal grand- father, who somewhat prophetically named him "Fy nhyn dyfodol I"—that is, "My man of the future." When he was five years old his grand- father died suddenly; as hia daughter described it, "he fell dead ia the garden." The home was broken up, and the child was placed with one Richard Price and his wife, who lived in the Bowling-green in Denbigh Castle. Shortly after- wards the son of this man, also named Richard Price, carried him on his back from Denbigh to the St. Asaph Union Workhouse, where he was brought up and bore the name of his father, John Rowlands. His subsequent career may be read in a little book published some years ago by Mr. Camden Hotten, of Piccadilly, entitled, if I recollect aright, "H. M. Stanley, Story of his Life, by Cadwalladr Rowland." The name of Stanley is derived not, as stated by your correspondent, from a lady who adopted him, but from a storekeeper in whose service he lived when he first arrived in America. His moth i r died in her sixty-third year on March 23, 1886, and was buried in the church- yard of Bodelwyddan, near St. Asaph. It is recorded on her coffin plate in these simple words that she was "Mother of 11. M. Stanley, the .African explorer."
SMOKING CONCERT AT THE WAR- RINGTON CONSERVATIVE CLUB.

Last evening a well-attended smoking concert, was held at the Conservative Club, Sankey-street. The chair was taken by Mr. Jelin Tinsley, who, inn few openingremarks, referred to the great services which had been rendered by Mr. George Woods In the getting up of those smoking concerts. He saw from the programme that those who ministered to their enjoyment at the lass concert Were conspicious by their absence, but he had no doubt that Mr. Woods bad some agreeable changes for them that evening. He (the chairman) had come with the intention of enjoying himself, and he hoped the audience would do the same. (APplause.) The musical part of the programme was than proceeded with, the first item being a glee, "By Celia's Arbour," by the West Derby quartette, which was capitally rendered. A comic song, "The Tailor's Feast," was next successfully given by Mr. Harry Antonie, and then the quartette again appeared in the part song, "The Sailor's Song." Mr. James F. Calder was warmly applauded for a fine interpretation of "The Village Blacksmith ; and some amusement was caused by Mr. Harry Antonie's Lancashire sketch, "Our Johnny, a gradely Lancashire lad," with the song, "I fancy I can see her now." The part song, " Star of the Summer Night," having been given by the quar- tette, Mr. Albert Carnidge won a recall by his song, "The Message," when he gave "Once again •' with equal success. The first part of the programme was concluded by a comic song, "Grandfather Shoreham," by Mr. Antonie. This song was also so successful as to secure an encore, in response to which Mr. Antonie gave sm amusing imitation of various actors. The second part was carried out by the same artistes with marked success. For their opening piece, the part song "The banks of Allan Water," the quartette were honoured with an encore, and subsequently the recalls were numerous and hearty. The audience marked its appreciation by vociferous applause of a particularly able rendering of the song "The last watch," by Mr. Alfred CamidFte; while Mr. Antonie had to give several repetitions for his humorous sketches and imita- tions. Altogether the concert passed off in a most successful and creditable manner.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

Subterranean disturbances were felt at Emsworth, Hants, at eleven o'clock on Friday. Sir William Jenner's condition has much improved, though he is still unable to visit patients. Mr. Bright slept five hours on Thursday night, and his condition on Friday was similar to that on the previous day.

The funeral of Mr. P. 11. Muntz, formerly a member of Parliament for Birmingham, took placp on Friday at Leamington. The Midlothian Liberal Committee have forwarded to Mr. Gladstone an address congratulating him on attain- ing his 79th _birthday. Lady Tollemache has been removed from Peckforton Castle, Chester, to London, in order to have close medical attention in the serious illness that has recently befallen her.
A" Times" telegram, dated Zanzibar, Friday, says intelligence has been received there of the safety of all the missionaries at Urambo, Mywapwa, and Mbora. The Germans have fortified the hill at Boma.

Mr. Gladstone, in a letter published in the " Tablet " , expresses the opinion that the. question of the present position of the Pope is of such importance as to merit the intervention of international arbitration. Loss OF A VESSEL AND ALL HANDS.—The Ada, a vessel plying from Exeter to Harwich, was totally wrecked on Thursday near Abbotsbury, Dorset. All the crew were lost, together with the cargo, which was composed of petroleum. FATAL RESULT OF A QUARREL.—TWO men, named Mannion and Walsh, quarrelled at a public-house at Chesterfield on Thursday night, and crossed the river Hipper to fight in a field beyond, when, it is alleged, one : pushed the other into the river, and both disappeared. Lord Dufferin, late Viceroy of India, arrived at Brindisi from the East on Friday morning with Lady Dufferin and family. His Excellency left at nine o'clock for Naples. The appointment of his lordship as ambassador to Italy appeared in last night's" Gazette." SHOCKING TEAGE'DY IN BIRMINGILI)I.—On Friday morning a man named John Cobb, a burnisher, living ' in Burchell-street, Birmingham, poisoned his wife with cyanide of potassium, and then swallowed a dose him- self. The dead bodies were afterwards discovered in the house by the police. Cobb had been drinking, heavily during the Christmas. FLOODS IN THE MIDLANDS.—Twenty-four hours heavy and almost incessant rain resulted in tremendous floods on Friday in Warwickshire, Leicestershire, and other parts of the midland counties. Rivers have in many places overflowed their banks, inundating the land for long distances on either side. Hundreds of acres of low lying land—meadows—are wholly or partially sub- merged, and in some of the country districts roads are impassable to pedestrians. EXECUTION OF PRADO. The man Prado, who, after a long trial, was found guilty of murdering Marie Ague ant, and sentenced to death, was executed ,at half-past seven in Paris on Friday morning. He met his death with courage, but made no confession, and declined the ministrations of the prison chaplain.

div.head: 'THE CRISIS IN FRANCE.
div.p: 'THE CRISIS IN FRANCE.

PARTS, FRIDAY.-At a council of Ministers, held to- day, it was decided that the elections in the vacant Paris district shall take place on the 27th January. General Boulanger will be the Opposition candidate. RECONNAISSANCE AT SUAKIM.

General 6-r—e-nfell, with the Welsh contingent, a regi- ment of Souclanese, and the Mounted Infatrry, marched out from Suakim on Friday morning, and advanced four miles into the country. Very few of the enemy were seen, and these all retired upon Flandoub. The forces eying filled some wells from which the rebels were drawing supplies of water, returned to camp. TERRIBLE EXPLOSION. EIGHTEEN REPORTED KILLED. A d, kiatch which has' revihed Rome from Messina reports a terrible catastrophe at the Camp Degli. Dur- ing some experiment with a new explosive, which is said to be an English invention, a boinO exploded with , terrible results. Sixteen of the soldiers present at the trial are said to have been killed outright, as well as the captain and the captain's wife, the latter assisting her husband with the experiment. No less than twenty soldiers were wounded more or leas severely. The cause of the explosion, has not transpired. SUPPOSED LOSS OF TWO STEAMERS.

The steamer Richard Arming, which arrived at Ply- mouth on Friday with her main shaft broken, after a perilous voyage from Gibraltar, which has occupied eleven days, brings Information which points to the probable loss of two large steamers. The Richard Arming left Gibral- tar in company with a Greek steamer, but the latter was throw ii on her beam 'eti4S, her deek houses flooded and so damaged that she had to turn back. She has not since been heard of. Subsequently the Richard Anning fell in with another large steamer, and kept company with her for, some days, but being, compelled by the force Of the hurricane to turn to, the stranger : was suddenly lost sight of, and is supposed to have foundered. This was on Sunday last, when the force of I the wind *as terrific, and the sea was running in moun- tains. THE MISSISSIPPI DISASTER. '

div.head: JIM GIVENS' HEROISM.
div.p: JIM GIVENS' HEROISM.

- . NEW Youx, TITCrESDAY.—The latest reports of the Mississippi steamer disaster give an account of a remark-. able deed of heroism, performed by a deck hand named Jim Givens. When the burning steamer touched the bank and bounded away the pilot left the wheel and sprang overboard. Givens quickly realised that the salvation of all onboard depended upon the steamer being brought back to the bank. The pilot-house was sur- rounded by flames, but the brave fellow sprang to the wheel, and brought ' the steamboat's head again to the bank, and, in order to keep her there, made the wheel fast in proper position. The fire swept over the pilot-house, and he was imprisoned by the flames. To escape it was necessary to rush through a wall of fire He made a dash for the side of the vessel, and, although frightfully burned, succeeded in reaching it. With his clothing all ablaze he jumped into the river, and struzgled to the bank, where he was pulled ashore by willing hands in a horribly burnt and exhausted state. He died after indescribable agony a few hours tater.— . Dailv News.

WARRINGTON. GUN ACCIDENT.—On Christmas Day, Mr. William Horton, farmer, Thelwall, was treated at the Infirmary for injuries received to the hand. Ile was shooting over his land when the breech of the gun flew out, shattering his thumb. HOLY TRINITY Cutrums.—On Sunday collections were made in this church in aid of the choir and organ expenses. The Vicar of Thelwall, the Rev. T. Pym Williamson, preached to a large congregation in the evening. "Tin YEOMEN OF TUB GUARD."—This the latest of the Gilbert and Sullivan extraordinary successes, will be presented in Warrington for the first time on Friday and Saturday next. It is hardly neces- sary to say that the visit of Mr. D'Oyly Carte's Opera Company is anticipated with pleasure by the admirers of Gilbert and Sullivan, and that crowded honses may be expected. FOOTBALL CLUB.—ANNUAL BALL—The eighth annual ball in connection with the Warrington 4 Football Club was held in the Co-operative Hall on Wednesday evening. The ball was again very largely attended. Messrs. G. Smith, C. R. Adamson. arid 'H. Ashton acted as misters of ceremonies, these gentlemen having also • formed a sub-com- mittee to carry out the necessary arrangements. Dancing was kept up with zest till well into Thursday morning: • Tins BIRTH AND ORATE RAVI OF WARRINGTON —For the week ending Saturday, December 22nd, 1888. The mean tpmperature was 41-3 Fahren- heit, and therefore 6.6 deg. warmer than the pre- ceding week. The maximum temperature, 51 Fahrenheit, was recorded on the 20th inst., and the minimum temperature, 26 Fahrenheit, on the 19th inst. The rainfall measured .12in. The general direction of the wind was south- east. During the week, which was the 51st of the current year, 33 births and 22 deaths were registered. The death rate from all causes was equal to 23-7 per thousand, against 14.8, the average of the previous four weeks, and against 30.8 the corresponding Week of last year. The deaths included 1 from scarlet fever, 1 from thrush fever, 3 from premature birth, 1 from old age, 3 from brain disease, 7 from lung disease. 7 cases of scarlet fever were reported under the requirements of the Act of Parliament.— Joins 11. GonsrAme Medical Officer of Health. PROPOSED ECONOMIC BUILDING SOCIETY.—A meeting for the consideration of a proposed Eco- nomic Building Society, to be started in Warrington, was held in the Co-operative liall,last evening week. There was a good attendance, the chair being-occu- pied by Mr. Thomas Morris, who was supported by Messrs. J. Peers, (originator of the societies), H. J. Loegton, Thomas Birchen, W. Walker (secretary), Joseph Albinson, Joseph Dobson, J. T. Hulse, Samuel Jones, Joseph Mounfield, junr., John Roberts, James Smethurst. The Chairman, before calling upon Mr. Peers to explain the rules of the society, said he personally recommended the society to the notice of his hearers. • He believed that members of the society easily made from 4 to 4-it per cent—Mr. Peers said the societies were formed for the cultiva- tion of thrift, and he believed had done a great amount of work in the country. Co-operation was the only system for the preservation of thrift, and that was the principle involved in those societies. He then went on to explain the rules. At the con- clusion of Mr. Peers' address he answered several questions put to him to the satisfaction of the -majority of the audience. Votes of thanks were passed to the Chairman and speaker and the pro- ceedings terminated. We understand that after the meeting, a number of shares were taken up. CROFT BOARD SCHOOL.—The annual entertain- ment and prise distribution took place at the above school last evening week. The school- room, which had been tastefully decorated with Chinese lanterns, evergreens, mottoes, &c., was crowded, and the Rev. T. P. Kirkham, ALA., presided. A raised platform had been erected at the west end of the schoolroom, and upon it were seated upwards" of 40 of the elder scholars who were to take part-in the entertainment, and their bright faces and clean and neat appearance added greatly to the pleasant scene. The whole of the programme was rendered in a highly creditable manner by the scholars, and the manner in which thev. performed their respective parts reflected the highest praise on Mr. Ball, the head master, who thined them. The accompaniments were played by Mr. Ball (who also conducted) and Miss A. C. B. Owen, in excellent style, and the teachers (Miss, Ball, Miss Stretch, and Mr. Lewis Daintith) also rendered valuable assistance. During the interval between' the first and second parts of the programme, the echolars were supplied with coffee and buns, and at the conclusion the Chairman dis- tributed tile prizes, consisting of choice and useful books, to the scholars who had passed the various standards at the Gevernment inspection in April ' last and also for good attendance. I _ . . .

Yea BOO'I'S AND Sithms or every description go to Haynes', Horsemarket-st., Warrington. —Advt. ORFOILD DAY SCHOOL. Last evening week, the annual prize distribution to the childten attending the Orford Church Day Schools took place in the schoolroom. There was a large atten- dance of parents and friends, amongst whom were Mrs. Beawont, Mrs. Jackson, Miss Hill, the Rev. S. Wilkinsori,Rev. I. and Mrs. Phillips,Rev. T. Emmott, Mr. Mortimer, Mr. Percy Mortimer, &c. The pro- ceedings opened with the performance of a school cantata, entitled "The White garland," which was very creditably rendered by about 45 of the scholars. At the conclusion of the. cantata the Rev. I. Phillips mentioned that, in April the Diocesan . Inspector visited the school, and gave a good and encouraging report, commending especially the following scholars :—Mary Swindells, P. M. Wilson, Mabel A. Cann, Ellen Ryder, Robert Corbett., John W. °leave, Tom Roberts, Tom Antrobus, Peter Ingham, Charles Povey, Ernest Hatton, William , Hatton, Joseph Sadler, Elizabeth Knott, Mary Knott, Emily Povey, Jessie Monks, Sarah Sollory, John Jepson, George Trevor, Hugh England, Margt. Delahay, Edith J. Cann. All of the above were entitled to prizes and certificates. On July oth the Government inspection took place. Full grant was earned for geography, grammar, singing, and cookery, besides the grant for the elementary sub- jects. The total grant reached over RI per head. The list of prizes included certificates and awards for regular attendance, and had been gained by the following t—Edith Cann, W. Knowles, Robert Ing- ham, Emily Higham, Lily Fisher Taylor, Elizabeth Ingham, William Andrews, John Sollory, Tom Cor- • belt, Sarah A. Higham, John Hall, Alice Leigh, Horace Wilson. The prizes for attendance were then diatiibuted by Mrs. Beamont, and those for efficiency in religious knowledge ,by the Rev. S. Wilkinson. Votes of thanks concluded the pro- ceedings. "MY SWEETHEART AT THE PUBLIC II ALL.— The popular play of "My Sweetheart " has again scored a success at the .Warrington Public Hall, the audiences always being large, that of Boxing night packing the hall in every part. Messrs. Miller and Elliston have at present a particularly able and well-balanced company. The part of Tina Hatzell, upon which the success of the piece so largely depends' is taken with notable success by Miss 1 Marie Montrose Her acting is at once lively and I natural, and her dancing and singing kracef al and Ipleasing. Together with Miss Montroile. Mr. Agust us Cramer, as Tony Faust, quickly installed himself as a favourite with the audience and his performances invariably i won cordial applause. Miss K. M. Neville, as Mrs. Fleeter, and Mr. Berkeley Perkins, as Dr. Oliver, reach a high pitch of excellence in the representation of the characters they take and Miss Jane Grey is a decided success as Mrs. Hatzell. As Dudley llarcourt, Mr. E. Irughnott is the cause of endless amusement, and he may be said to have reached. something like perfection in this impersonation. Mr. Percy Lessey undoubtedly makes a capital Joe Stilt well, and his dramatic appearances on the stage are always the signal for applause. Harold Bartlett, the gaMbler, finds a ' capital exponent in Mr. George Herbert.. It may be mullioned that on Wednesday afternoon the inmates of the Workhouse, and the scholars at the Blue Coat and the radiate Industrial Schools, were present at an entertainment on the generaus invitation of Messrs. Miller and Elliston. It may be added that the children from the Blue Coat School numbered 55, from the 'Padgate schools 138, and. about 100 men, women, and children from the Workhouse were also present. The band of the Blue Coat School played" a selection of music between each act, and, during one of the intervals, buns and oranges were suppliedto inmates of the three institu-. tions at the expense of Messrs. Miller and Elliston. The children from the Blue Coat School, Industrial School, and the inmates of the Workhouse were under the cara_of Mr. and Mrs. Rose, Mr. and Mrs. Mines, and Mrs. Ward respectively.

LAMM and •.fANTLEmEN,—Since issuing my address as a candidate to represent your division on the Coatiaty circumstances have come to my knowledge which wilL.prevent me further seeking that honour. It appears that by, a Section of the Municipal Corporation Act of 1882, whichle incorporated with the Local Government Act of 1888, that any person who has any share or interest in any contract with .the Council is disqualified from ..being a member. . For many years suy,firm have supplied the various Highway Boards in the County, with large quantities of stone. and as the main roads are now to pass into the hands of the County Council, and hereafter .to be maintained by tliem, we should (in the event of my teing elected) be precluded from tender- ing for any supply forthe future. As this is a matter of. serious importance to us, I feel bound to withdraw my candie..4ature, though I assure you it is with the greatest reluctanee. ,as I should have felt proud to have been your first representative on this new and important body.
